title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors
bodyText:
In a one- or two-family dwelling, including a manufactured home, West Virginia requires an operational smoke detector near each sleeping area. The owner must provide, install and replace it, and where the owner does not live there the tenant must do routine maintenance on it. If a deaf or hard-of-hearing person lives in a dwelling you rent out, you must, on a written request by or for that person, install a smoke detector with a light signal; a sprinkler system installed under the State Fire Code and State Building Code may be provided instead of smoke detectors.

An AC-powered carbon monoxide detector with battery backup is required in a newly built residential unit with a fuel-burning heating or cooking source, and in apartment buildings, boarding houses and one- and two-family dwellings intended to be rented, in a common area open to the public or in the sleeping rooms next to, above and below rooms with permanently installed fuel-burning appliances; one is also required in a unit connected to a newly built garage, shed or barn with a fuel-burning source, and in newly built apartment buildings and one- and two-family rentals detectors must be hardwired with battery backup.

The statute does not say who maintains a carbon monoxide detector, so plan to do it yourself. A violation is a misdemeanor (fines of $250, then $750, then $2,000), and a city or county may impose greater duties. A violation may not be used as evidence of negligence in a civil damages case, and may not be a defense in a case involving an insurance policy. No statute sets smoke detector rules for apartment buildings or a fee for a tenant who disables a detector, so charge a tenant who damages or removes one only the actual cost of repair or replacement; building-wide rules come from the State Fire Code and State Building Code; the State Fire Code adopts NFPA 1 and NFPA 101 (2021 editions), and itself bars anyone from disabling a fire warning system.

title: Heat and Hot Water
bodyText: If a dwelling unit is supplied by direct public utility connections, you must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April. The duty does not apply where the unit is built so that its running water, heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control. The statute does not define reasonable heat or set a temperature, and it applies the same way to every kind of residential tenancy. Whether you meet the duty when the tenant holds the utility account for a separately metered unit is not settled by statute, so say clearly in the lease who arranges and pays for heat and hot water.

title: Landlord's Repair Duties
bodyText:
For residential property, you must:
- deliver the dwelling unit and surrounding premises in fit and habitable condition at the start of the tenancy and keep them that way
- keep the property in line with applicable health, safety, fire and housing codes
- make all repairs needed to keep it fit and habitable
- keep in good and safe working order the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, that you supply or must supply by written or oral agreement or by law.

In a building with more than one living unit, you must also keep common areas under your control clean, safe and in repair and provide appropriate facilities for removing ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste. The code and repair duties do not cover a code violation caused by the fault of the tenant, the tenant's family or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent, or repairs needed primarily because of that person's lack of reasonable care.

You are not required to make repairs while the tenant is behind on rent, but if your lease gives you a greater duty than the statute, the lease controls; the Landlord Maintenance clause this library uses for West Virginia promises repairs without an exception for unpaid rent, so if you use it, do not rely on the unpaid-rent excuse. The statute sets no repair deadline and no reporting procedure, so say in the lease how tenants should report problems.

title: Shifting Repairs to the Tenant
bodyText: No West Virginia statute says whether a lease may shift your statutory repair and habitability duties to the tenant or have the tenant waive them, and none sets a procedure, such as a separate signed agreement, for doing so. The habitability statute excuses you only where the tenant, the tenant's family or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent caused the code violation or the need for repair, and it says a lease that gives you a greater duty controls; it does not say a lease may reduce your duties. Whether a court would enforce a reduction or waiver is a question of case law, so keep tenant maintenance terms to routine tasks and do not use them to take away the statutory duties. A tenant's promise to leave the premises in good repair means returning them in good and substantial repair, reasonable wear and tear excepted, and does not oblige the tenant to rebuild or pay for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence unless other words in the lease show that intent.

title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets a tenant repair and deduct, withhold rent, pay rent into escrow or end the lease because you did not make repairs, and no statute sets a notice procedure or deadline for repair requests. In an eviction for unpaid rent, though, the tenant may answer that you breached a material covenant on which the duty to pay rent depends, and the court must then hold a hearing on that issue; a tenant who asks for and gets a continuance must pay the rent coming due into court. If buildings are destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence, rent is reasonably reduced until you rebuild unless the lease provides otherwise, and if you do not rebuild within a reasonable time the tenant may surrender possession and owe no further rent. A tenant who wins an eviction appeal after the lease term has ended gets money damages only, unless the case involves title, retaliatory eviction or breach of warranty. Other remedies for breach of your habitability duty, such as damages or rent abatement, depend on case law; the magistrate court's answer form lets the tenant check a defense that the premises are defective and violate the warranty of habitability. Ask tenants to put repair requests in writing and keep records.

title: Substitute Housing
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires you to provide or pay for substitute housing when the rental becomes unlivable, whether from fire, repairs or code enforcement. If buildings are destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence, the tenant gets a reasonable rent reduction unless the lease provides otherwise, and may surrender possession and stop owing rent if you do not rebuild within a reasonable time; the lease's Fire or Casualty Damage terms apply.

title: Rent Limits During a Declared Emergency
bodyText: Once the Governor or the Legislature declares a state of emergency, it is unlawful in the area covered by the declaration to rent or offer rental housing leased on a month-to-month term for more than 10 percent above the price you charged on the 10th day before the declaration, unless the increase comes directly from added costs, and then only up to 10 percent above your cost plus your customary markup. The limit lasts for the whole emergency or 30 days after the declaration, whichever is longer; under a declared state of preparedness it applies only to items the proclamation names, and the Governor reviews the covered goods every 15 days. A violation is an unfair or deceptive act under the consumer protection act and a misdemeanor (fine up to $1,000, jail up to one year, or both). The statute's definition of housing names only month-to-month rentals, not week-to-week or fixed-term leases. No West Virginia statute sets other landlord duties after a disaster, such as debris removal or rent during an evacuation; the lease's casualty terms and the rent-reduction statute govern damage.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: No West Virginia statute generally addresses renting the same unit to two tenants, except the reletting rule below. You must deliver the dwelling unit in fit and habitable condition at the start of the tenancy, so confirm a prior tenant has left before committing the unit to a new one; the lease's possession-delay terms govern if you cannot. After a tenant abandons with rent unpaid and you relet under the statutory abandonment and reletting notice, a new tenant who leased under that notice keeps possession if the new lease was made before the original tenant notified you in writing of the intent to resume possession and paid or tendered what is owed.

title: Which Fire, Building and Housing Codes Apply
bodyText: West Virginia's habitability statute requires you to keep a rental in line with applicable health, safety, fire and housing codes, but the codes themselves are not in the statutes. The State Fire Code, a legislative rule of the State Fire Commission, has the force of law statewide as a minimum standard; a stricter local fire ordinance governs only if the Fire Commission has approved it. It does not apply to buildings used wholly as dwellings for no more than two families, though the smoke and carbon monoxide detector statute still does. The State Building Code applies only in counties and cities that adopt it, and only prospectively. Counties may adopt building and housing codes, cities may regulate construction and unsafe buildings, and local boards of health administer housing sanitation and may adopt local health rules with county or city approval. The State Fire Marshal may order an owner to repair or demolish a hazardous building within 30 days, and the cost can become a lien. No state health rule sets standards for ordinary rental housing; ask your local health department whether it has adopted local housing rules (see Local Health Department Rules). Check with your city or county; the Fire Commission's two rules were read (see Which Fire and Building Code Editions Apply for the editions they adopt), but the model codes they adopt and local codes were not.

title: Small Landlords
bodyText: West Virginia's landlord-tenant statutes do not change your duties based on how many units you own. Some rules turn on the building instead: common-area and garbage duties apply in buildings with more than one living unit, and the statutory smoke detector rule covers one- and two-family dwellings. Fair housing law applies to all dwellings, but the state discrimination rules largely do not reach renting rooms in a rooming house where you live with no more than four rooms rented. For familial status only, there are two exemptions: a single-family house rented by a private individual owner who owns no more than three such houses, without a broker or anyone in the business of renting and without discriminatory advertising; and units in a building for no more than four families where you live in one of them.

title: Quiet Enjoyment
bodyText: No West Virginia statute reads a covenant of quiet enjoyment into every lease. If your lease contains one, the statute says it has the effect of a promise that a tenant who pays the rent and keeps the lease's covenants shall peaceably possess and enjoy the premises for the term without any interruption or disturbance from any person whatever; its legal scope is then decided by the rules of law and the parties' intent, which is case law. Because those words are broad, think carefully before adding such a covenant. A tenant may enforce the lease's covenants against a later buyer of the property as against you. Whether a covenant of quiet enjoyment is implied without express words is a question of case law. Separately, a person turned out of possession by a forcible or unlawful entry may sue to recover possession within three years.

title: Rent Reporting
bodyText: No West Virginia statute regulates reporting tenants' rent payments to credit bureaus, requires you to offer rent reporting, or bars requiring a tenant to enroll in a rent-reporting program. If you report an unpaid balance, keep it accurate: if West Virginia's consumer debt collection law applies to rent, it forbids falsely telling a credit reporting agency that a consumer is willfully refusing to pay a just debt.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: West Virginia has no general statute barring a residential landlord from raising rent, cutting services or evicting because a tenant complained about conditions or reported code violations. The eviction statute mentions retaliatory eviction only on appeal: a tenant who wins an appeal after the lease term has ended gets money damages, not possession, unless the case involves title, retaliatory eviction or breach of warranty. Fair housing law makes it unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone for exercising fair housing rights or helping someone else do so. The magistrate court's answer form for these eviction cases lets the tenant check a defense that the action was filed in retaliation for complaints the tenant made about the premises. How courts treat that defense is a question of case law, so document an independent reason for any action you take soon after a tenant complains.

title: Locks and Security Devices
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires deadbolts, door viewers or window locks, requires rekeying between tenants, or regulates lock-change requests or charges. Building, fire and local housing codes may set requirements for doors and exits.

title: Code Enforcement and Receivership
bodyText: Cities and counties may adopt ordinances to make owners repair, close or demolish dwellings that are unsafe, unsanitary or unfit for human habitation, charge the costs to the owner, and record them as a lien on the property. A city's code enforcement officials must give the owner reasonable advance notice and ask permission before inspecting, except in exigent circumstances; if the owner cannot be found or refuses, they may get an administrative search warrant, a copy of which goes to the owner and any tenant in possession five days before entry. A city may let its municipal court place a structure in receivership where the owner cannot be found or refuses entry and the building is salvageable but needs prompt repair, and a city may charge a registration fee on uninhabitable property that violates its building code. No West Virginia statute gives tenants a specific right to have a receiver appointed or to pay rent into escrow for repairs of an occupied rental; the general equity receivership statute is not tenant-specific, and whether tenants could use it is case law.

title: Billing Tenants for Shared Utilities
bodyText:
West Virginia's deposit law says a landlord may use submetering equipment, energy allocation equipment or a ratio utility billing system if the rental agreement so provides, so put any such arrangement, and how charges are calculated, in the lease. No statute sets how a shared bill must be split, caps administrative fees, or requires a particular disclosure form. At the end of the tenancy you may apply the security deposit to utilities that were billed to and paid by you and that the lease makes the tenant's obligation.

The Public Service Commission's rules bar reselling water, and bar electric utilities from selling electricity for resale, unless the reseller is itself a public utility; whether billing tenants by submeter or formula counts as resale depends on Commission decisions, so for water and electricity include the service in the rent or have tenants take it in their own names unless the Commission or a lawyer confirms otherwise.

title: When the Utility Account Is the Landlord's
bodyText: No West Virginia statute gives tenants notice or a right to pay the utility and deduct it from rent when a utility account in your name is about to be shut off, and no statute requires a utility to notify the owner before disconnecting a tenant's own service. If the dwelling unit is supplied by direct public utility connections, though, you must supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April (unless generated by an installation in the tenant's exclusive control), so keep any account you hold current. If the lease makes the tenant responsible for utilities billed to and paid by you, you may apply the security deposit to the unpaid amount at the end of the tenancy. Under the Public Service Commission's rules, a tenant who holds an electric or gas account may name you to receive its shutoff notices (see Getting Copies of a Tenant's Utility Shutoff Notices), and if an account in your name for a master-metered building, or for a single-unit rental you do not live in, is about to be shut off, the utility must post a notice at the property at least five days before (for water and sewer, five days not counting weekends and holidays).

title: Window Guards
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires window guards, window stops or other window fall protection in rental housing, or a notice to tenants about them. Any such requirement would come from the State Building Code, the State Fire Code or local codes.

title: Belongings Left by a Tenant Who Abandons
bodyText: If a tenant who owes rent abandons the property, West Virginia law sets the steps. First post a written notice in a conspicuous place on the property requiring the tenant to pay the rent within one month; if it is not paid, you are entitled to possession and may enter, the tenant's right to the property ends, and you may recover the rent owed up to that time. To dispose of belongings left behind, give a second written notice, posted on the property and sent by first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, in an envelope marked "Please Forward", to the rental, to any post office box of the tenant you know of, and to any forwarding address you have. It must say the property is considered abandoned and that belongings must be removed from the property (or from where you stored them) by a stated date at least 30 days after mailing, or at least 60 days if the tenant has told you they are on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, or the tenant forfeits them and they become yours. If belongings worth more than $300 are not removed by that date and the tenant or a secured creditor tells you they intend to remove them, you must store them for up to 30 more days, provided they pay your reasonable storage and removal costs. The statute covers only a tenant who abandons while owing rent; no statute sets a procedure for belongings left by a tenant who owed nothing, so following the same notice steps is the safe course. Belongings left after a court-ordered eviction follow separate rules.

title: Abandonment, Reletting and Mitigation
bodyText:
When a tenant who owes rent abandons the property, the posted notice requiring payment within one month ends the tenancy if the rent is not paid, and the statute then lets you recover the rent owed up to the time you became entitled to possession. To keep the tenant liable for the rest of the lease, include in that same notice a further notice that, after taking possession, you will lease the property to someone else; the tenant then remains liable for the unexpired term for the difference between the rent you receive from the new tenant and the rent under the old lease, and on the lease's other terms.

If you give that notice, the tenant can still recover possession by notifying you in writing that they intend to resume possession and paying, or tendering, all rent arrears and other amounts then owed under the lease, unless you have already leased the property to someone else under the notice. No West Virginia statute says whether a landlord must otherwise mitigate damages by trying to re-rent; that is a question of case law, so making and documenting reasonable efforts to re-rent is the safe course.

title: Attorney Fees
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets a residential landlord recover attorney fees from a tenant, whether through a lease clause or in an eviction or rent case, and the lease in this library does not ask the tenant to pay them. West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law bars anyone collecting a consumer's obligation from collecting a fee or charge incidental to it unless both the agreement and a statute or regulation expressly authorize it, and from representing that the debt may be increased by attorney fees that cannot legally be added, with a penalty of $1,000 per violation, and the tenant may also be awarded attorney fees. That law can be read as treating a charge added because of a default or for collection, such as attorney fees, as incidental and needing statutory authority, which no statute gives for a landlord's attorney fees; a fee clause carries real risk. Statutes do give tenants attorney fees in some cases: when a landlord sues to enforce a lease term waiving security deposit rights, when a court allows them to a prevailing complainant in a fair housing suit, and in a suit for wrongful removal under the squatter-removal law.

title: Grounds for Eviction and Cure Periods
bodyText:
West Virginia's summary eviction procedure lets you petition to remove a tenant who is behind on rent, has breached a warranty or a covenant of the lease, or has deliberately or negligently damaged the property or knowingly let someone else do so. No West Virginia statute requires a notice or a chance to cure before you file on any of these grounds, in any kind of tenancy.

Three limits come from elsewhere:
- if the lease sets a time that must pass before you may re-enter, such as a cure period, a statute bars starting an ejectment or unlawful detainer case until that time has passed, so honor any cure or waiting period your lease gives before filing
- a tenant who has abandoned the property owing rent is handled by the one-month posted notice
- on a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program, federal law may require 30 days' notice to vacate (see the CARES Act row).

A tenant who simply stays after the lease ends is not on the summary petition's list of grounds; see the holdover row. This library's lease gives written notice and a cure period for curable breaches other than nonpayment of rent.

title: No Required Notice Before Filing for Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute requires a pay-or-quit notice, or any other notice, before you file to evict for unpaid rent; a summary eviction petition may be filed once the tenant is in arrears. The exceptions: if the tenant has abandoned the property, you use the posted notice requiring payment within one month; the federal CARES Act may require 30 days' notice to vacate for some properties (see that row); and you should honor any notice or waiting period your own lease promises. A tenant may defend by showing that you breached a material covenant on which the duty to pay rent depends.

This library does not offer a clause waiving a nonpayment notice, because there is no statutory notice to waive.

title: How Evictions Work in West Virginia
bodyText: Most West Virginia evictions use the summary procedure for wrongful occupation of residential rental property. The owner or the owner's agent files a verified (sworn) petition in the magistrate court or circuit court of the county where the property is, describing the property and the unpaid rent, lease breach or damage relied on; magistrate court can hear it so long as title to the property is not in dispute. The court sets a hearing 5 to 10 judicial days after filing, and you must immediately have notice of the hearing served on the tenant, under the civil service rule (the court's summons form lists the sheriff, a private process server, or certified mail) or by certified mail, return receipt requested, and then file the petition and proof of service. The tenant may serve a written defense within five days of receiving the notice and may raise any defense available in an ejectment or unlawful detainer case, and either side may elect a jury by giving the court written notice within five days after service. If the tenant has filed nothing by the hearing, the court orders immediate possession; otherwise it hears the case. The court may also enter judgment for rent due, and its order sets the date and time to vacate, after which the sheriff removes the tenant. Either party may appeal a magistrate court judgment to circuit court within 20 days by posting a bond, unless excused as unable to pay. Holding over after the lease ends is not one of the listed grounds for the summary petition; unlawful detainer is the procedure written for it (see the holdover row), and the squatter-removal law cannot be used against a current or former tenant.

title: Delays and Stays of an Eviction
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets a court postpone an eviction because of the tenant's hardship, the weather or the season. In a summary eviction, though, the court's order sets the time by which the tenant must vacate, taking into account whether the property is furnished or unfurnished, the possible relative harm to the parties and other relevant facts, and only after that time does the sheriff remove the tenant. Continuances are for cause only, and a tenant who gets one must pay into court the rent that comes due meanwhile. A party may appeal a magistrate court judgment to circuit court within 20 days, or ask the magistrate within 20 days to set it aside, and a timely appeal or motion stays enforcement; but the summary eviction statute says a tenant is not entitled to remain in possession during an appeal if the tenancy has otherwise expired. Expect delay when a tenant appeals, and get advice on how the two rules apply.

title: Eviction Court Records
bodyText: No West Virginia statute seals, expunges or limits public access to eviction court records, whether the case was a summary eviction or an unlawful detainer.

title: Tenants Who Stay After the Lease Ends
bodyText:
A tenant whose lease is for a fixed term must leave when it ends; West Virginia requires no notice from either side to end a tenancy whose term is to end at a set time. A tenant who stays on after their right has expired, without your consent, is in unlawful detainer, and you recover possession through an unlawful detainer case in circuit court or magistrate court, filed within three years, in which you can also recover damages for the detention, including mesne profits (the value of the use) for up to three years and any damage or waste.

The summary eviction petition lists unpaid rent, breach of a lease covenant and damage as its grounds; whether a holdover can be brought as a breach of the lease's promise to surrender possession is not settled by statute, and unlawful detainer is the procedure written for it. Do not treat a holdover tenant as a squatter: the squatter-removal law does not apply to a current or former lawful tenant, and a periodic tenant who holds over is not a squatter. Whether accepting rent after the term creates a new periodic tenancy is a question of case law; the lease's Holdover terms address it.

title: No Statutory Holdover Rent
bodyText:
West Virginia has no statute setting double rent or any other multiple of rent for a tenant who holds over. In an unlawful detainer case you recover damages for the detention, including mesne profits (the value of the use), special damages and waste, and in an action for rent or for use and occupation interest is allowed as on other contracts. This library does not offer a premium holdover rate clause: no statute authorizes one, whether a stated multiple would be enforced or struck as a penalty is a question of case law, and West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law can be read as treating a premium charged because the tenant stayed past the end of the lease as an added charge that needs statutory authority, which none gives.

The lease's Holdover terms let you recover actual damages, including the reasonable rental value for the time the tenant stays. No statute expressly forbids a holdover premium, but under one reading of the debt-collection law, collecting one could expose you to a $1,000 penalty for each violation; get advice before adding one.

title: Paying the Rent to Stop an Eviction
bodyText: In an ejectment or unlawful detainer case to recover the property for unpaid rent, if the tenant, or anyone else with a claim to the property, pays or tenders to you or your attorney, or pays into court, all the rent and arrears with interest and costs at any time before trial, the case must stop. Even after a judgment for possession is carried out, the tenant has twelve months to pay the rent in arrear with interest and costs, or to sue in equity for relief from the forfeiture, before losing all right to be restored, and a mortgagee or trustee of the tenant's interest has the same right. Whether these rules also apply to the summary eviction procedure is not settled by statute, though a tenant there may raise any defense available in ejectment or unlawful detainer. If a tenant offers everything owed, with interest and costs, before the hearing, get legal advice before refusing it.

title: Rent Paid Into Court and Counterclaims
bodyText: In a summary eviction for unpaid rent, the tenant may defend by showing that you breached a material covenant on which the duty to pay rent depends, and the court then holds a hearing on it. West Virginia's statutory repair duties do not require you to make repairs while the tenant is behind on rent, but that excuse applies only if the lease does not promise more, because a greater repair duty in the lease controls; this library's maintenance clause promises repairs with no exception for unpaid rent, so under it you remain responsible for repairs even while rent is owed. If a tenant asks for and gets a continuance, the court must require the tenant to pay into court the rent that comes due during it, and the court may pay out money paid in. A tenant may also file a counterclaim, which is tried with your case if it arises from the same transaction, and a tenant who does not file one can still sue on it later. In an ejectment or unlawful detainer case, a tenant who seeks an injunction against the case through a suit in equity must, within 30 days after your answer, bring into court, or deposit in a bank in the state to the credit of the case, the rent you swear is due and the costs. An appeal to circuit court requires a bond unless the appellant is excused as unable to pay.

title: Lockouts and Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: West Virginia's landlord-tenant statutes do not expressly ban lockouts or utility shutoffs by a residential landlord (its rules for manufactured-home lot rentals do), but the lawful ways to recover possession are a court case or, for a tenant who abandons owing rent, the posted-notice procedure. A court order for possession is carried out by the sheriff, and goods can be seized for rent (distress) only by the sheriff or a deputy sheriff under a magistrate's warrant. A person forcibly or unlawfully turned out of possession may sue within three years to recover it, without having to prove title, and recover damages. For units on direct public utility connections you must supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April, unless the tenant controls the installation. Do not change the locks, remove doors or belongings, or cut off utilities to force a tenant out; what else such conduct may expose you to is a question of case law.

title: Tenant's Belongings After an Eviction Order
bodyText: After a court grants you possession in a summary eviction, if the tenant has not removed all personal property by the date and time the order sets, you may: dispose of it without liability if the tenant tells you in writing that it is abandoned or if it is garbage; remove and store it, and dispose of it without liability after 30 days if the tenant has not paid your reasonable storage and removal costs and taken it back, or if the storage costs equal its value; or leave it on the property and dispose of it after 30 days if the tenant has not paid your reasonable costs of leaving it there and taken it back. If property worth more than $300 was not removed within those 30 days with the costs paid, and the tenant or someone holding a security interest in it tells you they intend to remove it, you must store it for up to 30 more days, provided they pay your reasonable storage and removal costs. You may apply the security deposit to reasonable removal and storage costs. The statute requires no separate notice before these steps and has no rule for pets or other animals left behind, and it does not cover belongings left after an unlawful detainer judgment; giving the tenant written notice and a reasonable chance to collect belongings, and keeping records, is the safe course.

title: No Just-Cause Requirement
bodyText: West Virginia has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule for residential rentals. You may let a fixed-term lease end on its last day without giving notice or a reason, and end a periodic tenancy by giving the required notice, without stating a reason. Limits that apply in particular situations: fair housing law bars refusing, ending or changing a tenancy because of a protected characteristic, and coercing, intimidating, threatening or interfering with a person for exercising fair housing rights; the summary eviction statute lets an appeals court restore a tenant whose lease has expired to possession where retaliatory eviction is at issue, and the court's answer form lists retaliation as a defense, though no statute defines retaliation for these rentals; and manufactured-home lot rentals have their own good-cause rules.

title: Criminal Activity and Eviction Speed
bodyText:
West Virginia has no separate expedited eviction or no-notice termination for criminal or drug activity by a tenant. The ordinary summary procedure is already quick, with a hearing 5 to 10 judicial days after filing, and is available when a tenant breaches a lease covenant, so a lease term against criminal activity lets you act on it promptly. Know your exposure as an owner: real property used to commit or facilitate a drug offense punishable by more than a year in prison can be forfeited to the state, unless the owner shows the act or omission happened without the owner's knowledge or consent, so act promptly once you learn of drug activity.

Nuisance laws that can close a property or require evictions are in the nuisance row.

title: Nuisance Laws and Rental Property
bodyText: West Virginia nuisance laws can reach a property owner whose rental is used for crime. A place where lewdness, assignation or prostitution is conducted or permitted is a nuisance: the owner, agent or lessee can be enjoined as maintaining it, and the court may close the place for a year; an owner may ask the court to release it by paying the costs and posting a bond for the property's full value to abate the nuisance, and the court may release it if satisfied of the owner's good faith, lack of knowledge of the use, and that reasonable care would not have revealed it. A place where alcoholic liquor is unlawfully made, sold or stored is a public nuisance that can be abated or closed. A building used by members of an organized criminal enterprise for qualifying offenses is a nuisance, and a court may order the owner or lessee to evict the persons using it and seal the premises. If law enforcement notifies you that a clandestine drug laboratory was found on your residential property, you must keep it unoccupied until the state certifies the remediation, or demolish it. Outside these proceedings, removing a tenant for criminal activity goes through the ordinary eviction process.

title: Drug-Free or Crime-Free Addenda
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires, forms or limits a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum. A lease covenant against criminal or drug activity can be enforced through the summary eviction procedure as a breach of a lease covenant, so a criminal-activity clause in the lease serves the same purpose. Federally assisted housing programs have their own required lease terms.

title: Lock Changes and Protective Orders
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets a tenant protected by a domestic violence order change the locks, or requires you to change them or to refuse a key to the person restrained. A protective order may grant the petitioner possession of the home the parties shared when the abuse occurred and order the respondent to stay away from the petitioner's residence; if a tenant shows you such an order, follow it, and get legal advice before giving a key or access to a person the order excludes, even one named on the lease.

title: Guarantors of a Lease
bodyText: A guaranty of a tenant's lease must be in writing and signed by the guarantor (or the guarantor's agent) to be enforced. Once the tenant is in default, a guarantor may give you written notice to sue; if you do not, within a reasonable time, sue every party to the lease who lives in West Virginia and is not insolvent and pursue the case diligently to judgment and execution, you lose your claim against the guarantor. A judgment against the tenant does not bind a guarantor who was not made a party and served, so name the guarantor in your suit. No West Virginia statute says whether a guaranty covers a renewal or extension of the lease; that depends on the guaranty's own words, so say in it whether renewals are covered. The consumer-credit cosigner notice rules apply to leases of goods, not to dwelling rentals. A guaranty is lawful; this library has no guaranty clause, because a guaranty is the guarantor's own contract, and a landlord who wants one can add their own after taking advice.

title: Waiving Exemptions From Collection
bodyText: A lease cannot make a tenant give up West Virginia's exemptions from collection: any waiver of the personal property exemptions is void and unenforceable, and a waiver of the homestead exemption is void except where it comes with a consensual security interest in the homestead itself that cannot be satisfied without encroaching on the exemption. A resident may hold exempt from execution or other process up to $8,000 in household goods, furniture, toys, animals, appliances, books and clothing held for personal or family use, up to $5,000 in one motor vehicle, up to $3,000 in tools of a trade and up to $1,100 on deposit in a federally insured bank, with a $15,000 total for those items. Rent can be collected by distress only through the sheriff or a deputy sheriff under a magistrate's warrant, within a year after it is due, and the code treats exempt property as protected from distress as well as from levy: it refers to property a debtor has listed and set apart as exempt from distress and levy, so expect a tenant to be able to claim the exemptions against a distress. This library does not offer an exemption-waiver clause, because such a waiver is void.

title: Tenants' Statutory Rights to End a Lease Early
bodyText: West Virginia statutes give a residential tenant, or the tenant's estate, these rights to end a lease early: when a tenant dies, an heir, personal representative, devisee or assignee may end the lease by written notice (see the tenant-death row); if the buildings are destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence and you do not rebuild as soon as you reasonably can, the tenant may surrender possession after that reasonable time and owe no further rent; and if the whole property is taken by eminent domain, the tenant's liability for rent ends unless the lease expressly provides otherwise. Federal law adds servicemember rights, which West Virginia extends to Guard members on state active duty for 30 days or more. No West Virginia statute gives tenants an early-termination right for domestic violence, illness, disability or a move to a care facility. The lease's Early Termination terms keep these rights.

title: Illness, Disability or Care-Facility Moves
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets a tenant end a lease early because of illness, disability, age or a move to a nursing home or assisted living. If a tenant dies, an heir or personal representative can end the lease (see the tenant-death row). Fair housing law requires reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling; whether that can require an early release from a lease is a question of case law, so take a tenant's request seriously and get advice before refusing it.

title: Servicemember Tenants
bodyText: West Virginia has no separate state statute letting servicemembers end a residential lease; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act does. A servicemember who signed the lease before entering service, or who later receives permanent-change-of-station orders or deployment orders for 90 days or more, may end it by written notice with a copy of the orders; for monthly rent the termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date, rent is prorated to that date, and you may not charge an early termination fee. The same right covers a lease signed on receipt of such orders when a stop-movement order then prevents occupancy (effective when the notice is delivered), a spouse or dependent within one year after the servicemember dies in service, and a servicemember who suffers a catastrophic injury or illness in service; the tenant still owes rent prorated to the termination date and other lease charges such as excess wear, and you must refund rent paid in advance within 30 days. West Virginia gives members of the West Virginia National Guard called to state active duty by the Governor for 30 days or more all of the protections of that federal Act. A magistrate may not enter a default judgment against a person in active military service who has not appeared unless the federal Act's procedures, including appointment of an attorney on the plaintiff's motion, have been followed. If a tenant who abandoned the property has told you they are on active duty, your notice about their belongings must give at least 60 days, not 30, to remove them.

title: Notice to End a Tenancy
bodyText:
To end a year-to-year tenancy, either side must give the other written notice at least three months before the end of a year of the tenancy. A periodic tenancy with a period shorter than a year, such as month-to-month or week-to-week, may be ended by the same notice or by notice of at least one full rental period before the end of a rental period: for month-to-month, at least a full rental month before the last day of a rental month; for week-to-week, at least a full week before the end of a rental week. No notice is needed from either side to end a lease whose term ends on a set date.

On a property covered by the federal CARES Act, though, give at least 30 days' notice to vacate, in writing to be safe, before you require the tenant to leave (see the CARES Act row). Notice to the tenant may be served on the tenant or on anyone holding the property under the tenant; notice from the tenant may be served on any owner or the owner's agent. These rules do not apply where the lease, by special agreement, fixes a different notice period or provides that no notice is to be given, so check your lease.

This library offers an optional clause, as that special agreement, letting either party end a periodic tenancy on a stated number of days' written notice before the end of a rental period; it does not offer a no-notice term, because that would let either side end the tenancy without warning. Give every notice in writing and keep proof of delivery.

title: Tenancies at Will
bodyText: No West Virginia statute defines a tenancy at will or says how much notice ends one. The notice statute covers year-to-year tenancies (written notice at least three months before the end of a year) and periodic tenancies shorter than a year (that notice, or notice of one full rental period before the end of a period), and requires no notice for a term that ends on a set date. Whether an arrangement with no set term or rent period is a tenancy at will, and what notice ends it, is a question of case law; if rent is paid by the week or month, treat it as a periodic tenancy and give at least one full period's written notice.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: When a tenant under a residential lease dies, an heir, personal representative, devisee or assignee of the tenant may end the lease before it expires by notice to you, hand-delivered or mailed postage prepaid. The termination takes effect on the last day of the calendar month that is two months after the notice is hand-delivered or postmarked: for example, notice mailed March 10 ends the lease on May 31. The tenant's estate still owes rent and other sums due before and during that two-month notice period, and the cost of restoring the property to its condition at the start of the tenancy, less ordinary wear and tear. No one can waive this right by contract or otherwise, and a lease term requiring longer notice is void. The statute applies to residential leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2012; it does not say how it reaches a month-to-month tenancy that began earlier, so honor it for every tenancy. Otherwise rent may be recovered from the tenant's heirs or personal representative as with other debts. No statute sets a procedure for a deceased tenant's belongings; work with the personal representative or heirs and keep records.

title: Minors in Eviction Cases
bodyText: No West Virginia statute bars naming a minor (a person under 18) as a defendant in an eviction or unlawful detainer case. A magistrate may not enter a default judgment against a minor unless the minor is represented in the case by a guardian ad litem, guardian or similar fiduciary, so name the adults who signed the lease or hold the tenancy, and name a minor only if the minor is a party to it. Whether a minor's own lease can be enforced against the minor is a question of case law; a promise made after turning 18 to pay a debt incurred as a minor can be enforced only if it is in writing and signed.

title: Fixing a Tenant's Breach Yourself
bodyText: No West Virginia statute gives a residential landlord the right to enter, fix a tenant's breach such as damage or uncleanliness, and bill the tenant for it. Your remedies are the lease's own terms, deductions from the security deposit after the tenancy ends for damage beyond reasonable wear and tear and other charges the lease provides for, a suit for damages, and the summary eviction procedure for deliberate or negligent damage. You are not required to make repairs made necessary primarily by a lack of reasonable care by the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent.

title: Utility Shutoffs at a Rental
bodyText: No West Virginia statute sets notice or protections aimed at tenants before a utility disconnects service at a rental, for example when a landlord who pays the bill falls behind; the Public Service Commission's rules require a regulated utility to post a shutoff notice at the property at least five days ahead when the landlord holds the account, so tenants can act. A municipal water utility, a public service district or a city sewer board may, under those rules, shut off water to a delinquent user ten days after the bill becomes delinquent, which happens when it is unpaid 20 days after it is due. Water may be shut off for an unpaid stormwater fee only after at least 10 days' written notice to the user and two attempts at personal contact in the 24 hours before; those protections belong to whoever is the user, who may be a tenant. For units on direct public utility connections you must supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April, unless the tenant controls the installation, so keep paid any service you are responsible for.

title: Bed Bugs
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a landlord to disclose bed bugs or a past infestation to a tenant, or sets bed bug treatment duties for rental housing. The state's only bed bug statute applies to hotels with ten or more bed chambers. Your general duties still apply: you must deliver and keep a residential unit fit and habitable, meet applicable health and housing codes, and make the repairs needed to keep it habitable, except where the problem is the fault of, or caused by a lack of reasonable care by, the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent.

title: Mold
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a landlord to test for mold, disclose mold to a tenant or prospective tenant, or follow a mold remediation procedure in rental housing. Mold can still matter under your duty to deliver and keep a residential unit fit and habitable and to meet applicable health and housing codes.

title: Radon
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a landlord to test for radon or disclose radon to a tenant. West Virginia's radon law licenses radon testers, mitigation specialists, contractors and laboratories; you may test or mitigate a building you own or lease yourself without a license, but you need a licensed professional to test or mitigate for you or to give professional advice on radon.

title: Flood Risk
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant or prospective tenant that the property is in a flood zone or has flooded before, or to tell tenants that their belongings are not covered by the landlord's flood insurance.

title: Former Drug Laboratories
bodyText:
If a law-enforcement agency notifies you that chemicals, equipment, supplies or precursors indicating a clandestine drug laboratory were found on your residential property, you are responsible for meeting the Department of Health's remediation standards (or you may demolish the building instead), and you must keep the property unoccupied from that notice until the Department certifies that the remediation meets its decontamination levels.

You, and any agent of yours, must also disclose the laboratory to any potential occupant, including where it was, the remediation plans, any related enforcement actions and whether the Department has issued a certificate of remediation completion; give this in writing before the tenant signs (see the Former Drug Laboratory Disclosure clause). Within 60 days of the notice you must test, begin remediation or demolish, and in a multi-unit building the units next to the laboratory must also be vacated and tested unless the Department allows otherwise. These rule duties are set to end on August 1, 2027 unless the rule is renewed.

Once remediation is certified, an owner who neither knew nor should have known of the illegal use is immune from suits by later renters based on that prior use, and the same immunity applies to such an owner who completes certified remediation voluntarily before any notice. A person convicted of possessing precursors to make methamphetamine whose actions made remediation necessary is liable for its costs, including reasonable attorney's fees and court costs to collect them.

title: West Virginia Lead Abatement Rules
bodyText:
West Virginia adds no lead paint disclosure of its own to the federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing. It does regulate lead abatement: only an individual holding the appropriate state lead license may carry out a lead risk assessment, inspection or abatement, and the owner of a residence where a lead abatement project is to occur must notify the Department of Health 10 days before the project starts and pay its fee. The homeowner exemption covers only a single-unit home occupied by the owner, not a dwelling occupied by tenants.

Renovation, remodeling and repair work not intended to permanently eliminate lead hazards, and temporary interim controls, are not abatement under this law, though federal renovation rules may still apply. The state may order reduction or abatement of identified lead hazards when they may result in child lead poisoning.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Stigma
bodyText: No West Virginia statute says whether a landlord must, or need not, tell a prospective tenant that a death, suicide, homicide or other crime occurred on the property, or that an occupant had an illness. The separate rule on former drug laboratories is covered under Former Drug Laboratories. Answer questions honestly; whether staying silent can be misrepresentation is a matter of case law.

title: Sex Offender Registry
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a landlord to tell tenants about the sex offender registry or that a registrant lives nearby, or to put a registry notice in the lease. Registry information is released only as the registry law provides: through community notification for sexually violent predators, a public list (at least quarterly) of people required to register for life, and court orders a county resident may petition for.

title: Military and Airport Zones
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a landlord to disclose that a rental is near a military installation, in an airport noise or accident potential zone, or in an airport overlay district.

title: Swimming Pools
bodyText: No West Virginia statute sets pool fencing, barrier, signage or safety-notice duties for residential landlords. The state health secretary may propose legislative rules on the design of swimming pools, whether publicly or privately owned; if your rental is in an apartment complex or condominium, the pool is a recreational water facility under the state health rule, and a pool that serves more than three families or paying guests is likely to be one too: you need a construction permit to build or renovate it and an operating permit, displayed at the pool, to run it, and the rule's design and operation standards apply. A pool at a single home housing no more than three families, used only by residents and their non-paying guests, is outside that rule. Any local building code may also apply.

title: Tenants After a Trustee's Sale
bodyText: When residential rental property is sold at a trustee's sale under a deed of trust, the purchaser may end the tenancy of a tenant holding an unexpired written lease that was never recorded, or was recorded after that deed of trust, by written notice: 90 days' notice, or notice given at least 30 days before the lease ends, whichever is shorter. A month-to-month or other tenancy may be ended by 30 days' written notice. These periods apply in place of the usual notice-to-quit rules. The notice must identify the property, the date of the trustee's sale, the book and page where the trustee's deed is recorded, the date the tenancy will end, and the purchaser with contact information; it is served by regular mail plus personal delivery, posting on the front door, or certified mail. The lease stays enforceable during the notice period, and if the tenant breaches it the new owner may use the summary eviction procedure. The statute does not address a lease recorded before the deed of trust. Factory-built home sites follow their own rules, and federal law may also protect tenants after foreclosure.

title: Pending Foreclosure
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a landlord to tell a prospective tenant that the property is in foreclosure or that the loan secured by it is in default. Because a buyer at a trustee's sale may end an unrecorded or later-recorded lease on short notice, telling applicants about a pending sale avoids disputes.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: If you convert a residential rental building into a condominium, cooperative or other common interest community under West Virginia's Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act, you (as declarant) and any dealer offering the units must give each residential tenant and subtenant in possession notice of the conversion, setting out their rights, together with the public offering statement, at least 120 days before they must vacate, by hand delivery to the unit or prepaid mail. No tenant may be required to vacate on less than 120 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste or conduct that disturbs other tenants, and the terms of the tenancy may not be changed during that period. For 60 days after the notice you must offer to sell each residential unit to the tenant who leases it; if the tenant does not buy, for the next 180 days you may not offer the unit on more favorable price or terms. Failing to give notice is a defense to an action for possession, and a lease may not be terminated in violation of its terms. These rights cannot be waived. These rules do not apply to a planned community or cooperative with 12 or fewer units and no development rights, or to a planned community whose declaration limits the average annual assessment on its residential units to $300 (adjusted for inflation), unless its declaration adopts the whole Act; and the purchase offer does not apply to a unit that will be nonresidential or whose boundaries will not substantially match the apartment.

title: West Virginia Fair Housing Act
bodyText: The West Virginia Fair Housing Act bars refusing to rent or negotiate, setting different terms or services, falsely saying a unit is unavailable, or making, printing or publishing any notice, statement or advertisement that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination, because of race, color, religion, ancestry, sex, familial status, blindness, disability or national origin. Its small-landlord exemptions are narrow: renting rooms in a rooming house you live in with no more than four rooms for rent; and, for familial status only, renting a single-family house if you own no more than three and use no broker or discriminatory advertising, or renting units in a building of up to four households where you live in one. Housing for older persons is exempt from the familial-status rule, religious organizations and private clubs have limited exemptions, reasonable occupancy limits set by law still apply, and you may refuse a person convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. Even where an exemption applies, don't advertise a preference. You may not threaten, coerce or retaliate against anyone for exercising these rights. A tenant may complain to the Human Rights Commission within one year or sue within two years; remedies include actual and punitive damages, attorney's fees and civil penalties. Federal fair housing law also applies.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Under the West Virginia Fair Housing Act you must make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices and services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a home, and you must permit reasonable modifications of the premises, at the tenant's expense, that may be necessary for full enjoyment of the premises. Where reasonable, you may condition permission for a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior at move-out, reasonable wear and tear excepted. For an assistance animal you may ask for documentation from a professional treatment provider of the disability-related need, but not for medical records or detailed information about the impairment; you may not unreasonably deny it, condition it on a fee, a deposit or the terms you apply to pets, or unreasonably delay your response, and you may deny it if there is credible evidence, based on an individualized assessment of the specific animal's actual conduct, that it poses a direct threat to others' health or safety, or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property, that no other reasonable accommodation can eliminate or reduce. You need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property, but you bear the burden of proving it. Buildings of four or more units first occupied after the Act's design deadline must meet accessible design rules (every unit if the building has an elevator, otherwise the ground-floor units).

title: Applications, Questions and Ads
bodyText: West Virginia makes it unlawful to make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement about renting a dwelling that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, blindness, disability, familial status, ancestry or national origin, or an intention to make one. Unlike its employment law, West Virginia's housing law has no separate rule on application forms or questions, but an application or screening question about one of those traits can itself be such a statement, so leave them out. For an assistance animal request you may ask for documentation of the disability-related need, but not for medical records or detailed information about the impairment.

title: Housing Vouchers and Source of Income
bodyText: West Virginia's fair housing law does not make source of income a protected class, and no West Virginia statute requires a landlord to accept housing vouchers or other rent assistance. A provision of the municipal home rule law lets a municipality regulate activities that arise from rental use only if the regulation applies uniformly to all properties, rented or not; whether that bars a local source-of-income protection is unsettled, so check local ordinances. A landlord who accepts a voucher must follow the program's rules and lease addendum.

title: Domestic Violence and Ending a Lease
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking end a lease early, or requires a landlord to change the locks for such a tenant. Unless the lease or a later agreement provides otherwise, the ordinary lease terms and notice rules apply; federal law may give protections in federally assisted housing.

title: Domestic Violence and Eviction
bodyText: No West Virginia statute bars a landlord from evicting, refusing to rent to, or refusing to renew a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, or makes that status a defense to eviction. A family court protective order may grant the victim possession of the residence the parties shared and order the abuser to stay away from the victim's residence; no statute says how such an order affects the lease, so get legal advice before acting against either party. Federal law may protect tenants in federally assisted housing.

title: Fee Disclosure and All-In Pricing
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires all-in rent pricing in advertisements, a first-page list of fees, or a separate fee disclosure for residential rentals. The written lease must still be clear and coherent, in everyday words and easily readable type, and organized and captioned, so list every fee and charge in the lease. A pet fee or application fee is outside the security deposit rules only if the tenant expressly agrees in writing that it is nonrefundable. A fee that is itself part of what the tenant agrees to pay (rent, reimbursement of a cost the lease makes the tenant's, or the price of an option the tenant chooses) is part of the tenant's obligation; a charge added because of a default or for collection, such as a late fee, returned-check fee, collection cost or attorney fee, needs a statute that authorizes it if West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law applies to rent.

title: Copy of the Lease
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a landlord renting a home or apartment to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, but give every tenant a signed copy. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson handles the lease for you, the licensee must give each person a true copy when that person signs and a copy to each party once the contract is accepted. An owner leasing their own property is not subject to the licensing law.

title: Rent Statement for Senior Tax Relief
bodyText: West Virginia gives property tax relief to residents aged 65 or older, including renters, whose gross household income in the prior year was not more than $5,000, counting 12 percent of the rent they pay as rent constituting property taxes. If a tenant claiming that relief asks, you must sign a statement of the gross rent the tenant paid for the calendar year (rent for occupancy only, excluding charges for utilities, services, furniture or appliances you provide). Willfully giving a false statement, or willfully failing to give one in time for the tenant to file a timely claim, is a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $50 for each violation. Claims are filed with the State Tax Commissioner between July 1 and September 30 for the prior year. No West Virginia statute otherwise requires you to tell tenants how much of their rent goes to property taxes.

title: Tenant Rights Summary
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a landlord to give a residential tenant a state summary of tenant rights, a truth-in-renting statement, or a copy of the landlord-tenant statutes with the lease. (Rentals of factory-built home sites in a rental community have their own rule requiring the statute's text with the agreement; they are outside this library. If you convert a rental building to a condominium or other common interest community, the conversion notice must set out the tenants' rights under that law; see Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums.)

title: Required Disclosures in West Virginia
bodyText: West Virginia requires few disclosures to residential tenants. Federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to pre-1978 housing. If the property or its subsurface was used to store, treat or dispose of hazardous waste and you owned it then or know of that use, the lease itself must say so (see the Hazardous Waste Disclosure clause); a former drug laboratory must be disclosed to any potential occupant (see the Former Drug Laboratory Disclosure clause); and a copy of any environmental covenant goes to persons in possession (see Contamination Disclosures). The written lease must be clear and coherent, in everyday words, in easily readable type with contrasting ink, and organized and captioned by section; a violation does not void the lease, but a tenant may demand a conforming lease and sue to reform it, and cannot waive that right. Submetering or utility allocation must be provided for in the rental agreement, and a pet or application fee is nonrefundable only if agreed in writing. A real estate licensee must disclose in writing, on the Real Estate Commission's form, whom the licensee represents. A declarant converting a building must give tenants a conversion notice, and on request you must sign a rent statement for a senior tax relief claimant. No statute requires an owner-identity notice, a move-in checklist or a tenant-rights summary, but a managing agent who does not disclose the owner's name is treated as the landlord under the deposit law.

title: Lease Terms West Virginia Voids
bodyText: West Virginia has no single list of forbidden lease terms; the rules are spread across several statutes. These terms in a residential lease are void or unenforceable: a term in which the tenant gives up rights under the security deposit law (if you sue to enforce one, the tenant can recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees); a term waiving the right of a deceased tenant's heir, personal representative, devisee or assignee to end the lease early, or requiring longer notice than the statute allows (leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2012; follow it for every lease); a waiver of the tenant's personal property exemptions from execution or other process; and a waiver of the tenant's right to ask for a lease rewritten in plain language. A term may not discriminate because of race, color, religion, ancestry, sex, familial status, blindness, disability or national origin. In a lease signed electronically, a party's right to refuse to do later transactions electronically cannot be waived. The habitability statute has no anti-waiver sentence, and no statute addresses a jury waiver, liability waiver or confession of judgment in an ordinary residential lease (the confession and unconscionability statutes are written for consumer credit sales, which can include a lease with an option to buy where rent is applied to the price, leases of goods and loans); whether courts enforce such terms is case law, and this library offers none of them. The Consumer Credit and Protection Act can be read to mean that a charge added because of a default or for collection, such as a late fee, returned-check fee, collection costs, attorney's fees, a holdover premium or interest beyond what the statute allows, may be collected only if both the lease and a statute authorize it (statutes authorize a reasonable late charge specified in the lease and a fee of up to $25 for a check, draft or order dishonored for insufficient funds or credit), while charges that are part of what the tenant agreed to pay, such as rent, an actual cost the lease makes the tenant's, or an early-termination fee for an option the tenant chooses, are not affected. Collecting a charge the law does not allow may be a prohibited debt collection practice, which can cost the tenant's actual damages plus a $1,000 penalty per violation (adjustable for inflation).

title: Penalties for Unlawful Lease Terms
bodyText: West Virginia has no general penalty just for including an unenforceable term in a residential lease. If you bring an action to enforce a term in which the tenant waives security deposit rights, the tenant can recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. The Consumer Credit and Protection Act's debt collection rules may reach unpaid rent; if they do, trying to collect an incidental charge not authorized both by the lease and by a statute or regulation, or saying the debt can be increased by fees that cannot lawfully be added, can cost $1,000 per violation (adjustable for inflation) plus the tenant's actual damages, and a court can award the tenant attorney's fees. You avoid the penalty if, before being sued or notified of the error, you notify the tenant and correct it within 15 days after discovering it (60 days if it affects more than two people); for a lease term, giving the tenant a corrected copy is enough. A tenant who is refused a plain-language rewrite can sue to have the lease reformed, but the lease is not void. Under this library's reading of the Consumer Credit and Protection Act, a charge added because of a default or for collection, such as a late fee, returned-check fee, collection costs, attorney's fees, a holdover premium or interest beyond what the statute allows, may be collected only if both the lease and a statute authorize it (statutes authorize a reasonable late charge specified in the lease and a fee of up to $25 for a check, draft or order dishonored for insufficient funds or credit), while charges that are part of what the tenant agreed to pay, such as rent, an actual cost the lease makes the tenant's, or an early-termination fee for an option the tenant chooses, are not affected.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: A confession-of-judgment clause (the tenant authorizes judgment to be entered against the tenant without a contested case) is void in West Virginia consumer credit sales, consumer leases of goods, consumer loans and rent-to-own transactions. A consumer credit sale can include a lease with an option to buy the home where all or a substantial part of the rent is applied to the price. No statute addresses a confession clause in an ordinary residential lease. Once a magistrate court case is pending, a tenant may offer to confess judgment, and the magistrate takes it in writing and enters judgment for the amount confessed plus costs. Whether a confession clause written into a residential lease is enforceable is a question for case law; this library includes no such clause.

title: Jury Trials and Jury Waivers
bodyText: West Virginia's Constitution preserves the right to a jury, if either party requires it, in suits at common law where more than $20 is in controversy. In a magistrate court eviction (wrongful occupation) case either side may elect a jury because the case involves possession of real estate, but under the magistrate court rules the election must be made in writing within 5 days after the summons and petition are served, or it is waived. No statute addresses a jury waiver written into a residential lease (the only statutory rule covers nursing home agreements); whether one is enforceable is a question for case law. This library does not offer a jury waiver.

title: Liability Waivers
bodyText: No West Virginia statute voids, or expressly permits, a residential lease term that excuses the landlord from liability or makes the tenant indemnify the landlord. The habitability statute puts duties on every residential landlord and says nothing about waiving them, and the state Constitution guarantees every person a remedy by due course of law for an injury to person, property or reputation; how courts treat liability waivers in leases is case law. For that reason this library's West Virginia parking, storage, renter's insurance and services clauses are the versions without "Landlord is not liable" sentences.

title: Unconscionable Terms
bodyText: West Virginia's unconscionability statutes are written for other transactions: consumer credit sales, consumer leases of goods and consumer loans; sales and leases of goods; rent-to-own agreements; and contracts governed by the common interest ownership act. Each lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable agreement or term. None names an ordinary lease of a home, though a lease with an option to buy, where all or a substantial part of the rent is applied to the price, can be a consumer credit sale. For an ordinary residential lease, whether a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term is case law. Separately, if the Consumer Credit and Protection Act's debt collection rules reach rent (the statutes do not say), you may not use unfair or unconscionable means to collect it.

title: Consumer Protection Act and Leases
bodyText: West Virginia's Consumer Credit and Protection Act makes unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce unlawful and defines a consumer transaction as a sale or lease to a natural person for a personal, family, household or agricultural purpose. Its plain-language rule expressly covers written agreements for the rental of residential space, but its private damages action belongs to a person who purchases or leases goods or services, and the statutes do not say whether renting a home is that. A consumer must give you written notice by certified mail and wait 45 days for a cure offer before suing under the Act. Its debt collection rules (no threats, oppression, unreasonable publicity or misleading statements, and no collecting incidental charges not authorized by both the lease and a statute or regulation) may also reach unpaid rent; treat them as applying. Under this library's reading of the Consumer Credit and Protection Act, a charge added because of a default or for collection, such as a late fee, returned-check fee, collection costs, attorney's fees, a holdover premium or interest beyond what the statute allows, may be collected only if both the lease and a statute authorize it (statutes authorize a reasonable late charge specified in the lease and a fee of up to $25 for a check, draft or order dishonored for insufficient funds or credit), while charges that are part of what the tenant agreed to pay, such as rent, an actual cost the lease makes the tenant's, or an early-termination fee for an option the tenant chooses, are not affected. The Attorney General may sue for repeated and willful violations, with civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation.

title: Tenant Information and Data Breaches
bodyText: No West Virginia statute specifically limits what a landlord may disclose about tenants or applicants. But if you keep tenants' or applicants' names linked to Social Security numbers, driver's license or state ID numbers, or financial account or card numbers (with any code needed for access) in unencrypted, unredacted computerized form, and an unauthorized person accesses and acquires that data in a way you reasonably believe has caused or will cause identity theft or fraud, you must notify each affected West Virginia resident without unreasonable delay. The notice must describe the kinds of information taken, give a phone number or website for questions, and give the major credit bureaus' contact information and how to place a fraud alert or security freeze; if you must notify more than 1,000 people, you must also notify the nationwide consumer reporting agencies. A vendor holding your tenants' data must tell you of a breach. Only the Attorney General enforces this, and civil penalties (up to $150,000 per breach) apply only to repeated and willful violations.

title: Immigration Status
bodyText: No West Virginia statute bars or requires asking a rental applicant or tenant about immigration status or citizenship. National origin and ancestry are protected classes under the West Virginia Fair Housing Act, so apply any identity, document or status policy to every applicant the same way. Any alien may own land in West Virginia as if a citizen; the 2025 foreign-ownership law reaches only businesses controlled by prohibited foreign parties (see Foreign Owners and Tenants).

title: Victim Information
bodyText: No West Virginia statute requires a landlord to keep a tenant's domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking information confidential, and no statute addresses victims in landlord-tenant terms at all. The state's Address Confidentiality Program lets certified participants use a substitute address with state and local agencies and courts; it does not bind private landlords. A domestic violence protective order may grant the victim possession of the residence the parties shared. Treat protective orders and victim information you receive as confidential.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: No West Virginia statute bars a lease term that penalizes a tenant, or lets you end the tenancy, because the tenant called the police or asked for emergency help, and none penalizes a landlord for a tenant's calls for service. This library's West Virginia clauses contain no such term; do not add one.

title: Tenant Unions
bodyText: No West Virginia statute protects residential tenants who organize or join a tenants' organization, or bars retaliation for it, in ordinary residential tenancies; the only such statute covers factory-built home site rentals. The eviction statute and the court's answer form treat retaliatory eviction as something a tenant can raise, but its scope is case law. The constitutional right of peaceable assembly limits government, not private landlords.

title: Tenant Screening
