bodyText: West Virginia has no statute listing a tenant's remedies when you break the lease or your repair duties, and none lets a tenant withhold rent, pay rent into escrow or end the lease because a health, lead or code violation goes unrepaired. The statutes give the tenant these routes instead. In a summary eviction for unpaid rent, the tenant may answer that you breached a material covenant on which the duty to pay rent depends, and the court must hold a hearing on it; a tenant who asks for and gets a continuance must pay into court the rent that comes due during it. A tenant sued in magistrate court may file a counterclaim, which is tried with your case if it arises from the same transaction, and may instead sue on it later. If buildings are destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence, rent is reasonably reduced until they are replaced unless the lease provides otherwise, and if you do not rebuild as soon as you reasonably can, the tenant may surrender possession and owe no further rent. A tenant who wins an eviction appeal after the lease term has ended gets money damages only, unless the case involves title, retaliatory eviction or breach of warranty. Whether a tenant may recover damages, reduce rent or end the lease for a breach of your habitability duties is case law, and the court's answer form lets the tenant raise the warranty of habitability. Fix reported problems promptly and keep records of requests and repairs.

title: Having the Tenant Do Your Repairs
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute sets conditions for a lease that has the tenant take over your repair or maintenance duties. There is no consideration requirement, no rule that the term be conspicuous or in a separate agreement, and no rule for repairs done in exchange for rent. Some limits come from the habitability statute itself and turn on facts, not on what the lease says. Your duty to supply running water, hot water and heat applies to units on direct public utility connections, and not where the unit is built so that its water, heat or hot water comes from an installation within the tenant's exclusive control.

Your common-area and garbage-facility duties apply in buildings with more than one living unit. Code violations caused by the fault of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent, and repairs needed mainly because one of them did not take reasonable care, are not your duty. The statute says a greater duty in your lease controls; it does not say a lease may shift its duties to the tenant, and whether a court would enforce a shift is case law.

This library therefore offers no clause shifting your statutory duties. Its routine-care terms keep those duties with you: Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness, the yard-care and snow-removal clauses, and Damage Caused by Tenant. If you want a tenant to do work for reduced rent, get legal advice, put the arrangement in writing, and keep making the statutory repairs yourself.

title: Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: West Virginia has no single list of tenant rights that a lease cannot waive; a few statutes each carry their own non-waiver rule. A lease cannot make the tenant give up rights or remedies under the security deposit law, the right of a deceased tenant's heir, personal representative, devisee or assignee to end the lease early, the tenant's exemptions from collection, the right to ask for a lease rewritten in plain language, or the right to refuse to do later transactions electronically. The habitability statute has no non-waiver sentence, and no statute says whether its duties can be waived, so do not rely on a waiver of them (see Waiving Habitability Requirements). No West Virginia statute sets special non-waiver rules for a home sold and leased back to the seller. Lease Terms West Virginia Voids sets out each of these rules and their consequences in full.

title: Promises to Repair or Improve
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule requires your promise to clean, repair or improve a rental to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. Your promises still bind you. The habitability statute makes you keep in good and safe working order the facilities and appliances you supply or must supply by written or oral agreement or by law, and a repair duty in your lease that is greater than the statute's controls.

The Consumer Credit and Protection Act lists a false promise made in connection with the sale or advertisement of goods or services as a deceptive practice; whether renting a home is covered is case law (see Consumer Protection Act and Leases). A licensed real estate broker or salesperson who rents or manages property for an owner can be disciplined for false promises likely to influence a person in a real estate transaction, but an owner renting its own property is outside that licensing law.

Write every promised repair or improvement into the lease with a completion date, using the optional Promised Repairs and Improvements clause, and put any later promise in writing too.

title: Ending a Lease When Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: No West Virginia statute lets you end a residential lease because repairs would cost more than they are worth, and none gives the tenant that right either. Your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable and make needed repairs does not have a cost limit. The one statutory exit after damage is the tenant's: if buildings are destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence and you do not rebuild or replace them as soon as you reasonably can, the tenant may surrender possession and owe no further rent, and until then rent is reasonably reduced unless the lease provides otherwise. The statute gives you no matching right to end the lease, so if you want one, the lease must provide it; this library's Fire or Casualty Damage clause lets you end the lease on written notice if you decide not to restore after a fire or other casualty. For damage short of a casualty, ending a periodic tenancy with proper notice, or not renewing a fixed term, are the usual routes.

title: No Small-Landlord Repair Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states let tenants pay rent into escrow when repairs are not made and exempt small landlords who say so in the lease. West Virginia has neither: no statute gives a tenant a rent-escrow remedy for repairs, and no statute exempts a landlord with few units from a repair remedy or requires the lease to disclose such an exemption. Your habitability duties are the same however many units you own, though common-area and garbage-facility duties apply only in buildings with more than one living unit. The only rent payments into court the eviction statute requires are rent coming due during a continuance the tenant asks for and gets. Nothing needs to go in the lease on this subject.

title: Repair Requests and Notice
bodyText: No West Virginia statute sets how a tenant must report a repair problem, what form the request takes, who may receive it, or how quickly you must respond. Your habitability duties are not conditioned on notice: the statute requires you to keep the unit fit and habitable, in line with applicable codes and in repair, without saying the duty starts only when the tenant tells you. Your lease may still ask tenants to report problems promptly and in writing, as this library's Maintenance & Repairs clause does, and it is wise to name where requests go. Because the statute does not depend on notice, do not count on a written-notice term to excuse a problem you knew about from a phone call, a text or your own inspection; whether a court would treat a lack of written notice as a defense is case law. In an eviction for unpaid rent, a tenant's defense that you breached a material covenant on which rent depends goes to a hearing whatever form any earlier complaint took. Keep a dated record of every request, however it arrives, and of what you did.

title: Carpet Cleaning and the Deposit
bodyText:
No West Virginia law addresses carpet cleaning at move-out, requires or forbids professional cleaning, or limits carpet or paint deductions by the age or condition of the carpet. The deposit law lets you apply the deposit, when the tenancy ends, to damages from the tenant's failure to follow the lease, less reasonable wear and tear, and to other damages or charges the lease provides for, listed in a written itemization. The law does not say whether cleaning carpets after ordinary use counts as reasonable wear and tear. So the library's optional Carpet Cleaning clause charges only for soiling or stains beyond reasonable wear and tear, at the actual reasonable cost.

A lease term making the tenant pay for professional cleaning in every case, whatever the carpets' condition, risks being treated as a charge for wear and tear or as an unenforceable waiver of deposit rights. Keep move-in photos or a condition record so you can show what changed. If damage exceeds the deposit and needs an outside contractor, send the tenant written notice of that within the deposit deadline; you then get 15 more days to send the itemization and repair costs.

title: No Move-Out Notice Condition on Deposit Refunds
bodyText: No West Virginia law lets you make the return of a security deposit depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, surrendering on a set date, or leaving a forwarding address. Your deadline runs from the end of the tenancy: deliver the deposit, less lawful deductions and with a written itemization, by the earlier of 60 days after the tenancy ends or 45 days after a new tenant moves in. You may hand it to the tenant or mail it to the tenant's last known address or the forwarding address the tenant gave you, and the law makes it the tenant's responsibility to give you an accurate address. If personal delivery is not reasonably possible and the mailed deposit or notice comes back undeliverable, hold it for six months and deliver it at your place of business, during normal business hours, within 72 hours after the tenant's written request. Your lease may ask the tenant for move-out notice and a forwarding address, and a periodic tenant who leaves without giving the termination notice the tenancy requires may still owe rent, which the deposit can cover. But a term that forfeits the deposit because notice or an address was not given risks being an unenforceable waiver of the tenant's deposit rights.

title: Deposits When a Victim or Co-Tenant Leaves
bodyText: West Virginia has no law letting a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking end a lease early, so it has no special deposit timing for such a tenant. It also has no rule on how one deposit is divided when one co-tenant leaves and the others stay. The ordinary deposit rule applies to every tenancy: deliver the deposit, less lawful deductions and with a written itemization, by the earlier of 60 days after the tenancy ends or 45 days after a new tenant moves in. The law ties that clock to the end of the tenancy and does not say whether one co-tenant's departure ends the tenancy for this purpose. If one co-tenant leaves while others stay, or you agree to release a tenant early, the cautious course is a written agreement signed by every tenant saying whether the deposit stays in place until the tenancy ends and who will receive the refund. In federally assisted housing, federal protections for victims may apply, so check those federal rules for any deposit timing they set..

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: West Virginia has no procedure, tenant election or fee for an expedited or early return of a security deposit, and none is needed: the deposit law's deadline is an outer limit. You must deliver the deposit, less lawful deductions and with a written itemization, by the earlier of 60 days after the tenancy ends or 45 days after a new tenant moves in, and you may always do it sooner. No statute authorizes or forbids a fee for faster processing. Because a deposit may be applied to other charges the lease provides for, a processing fee could come out of the deposit only if the lease names it. This library does not offer such a fee: no statute frames it, whether it is lawful rests on an unsettled reading of West Virginia's consumer protection law, and it gains a landlord little. If you want one anyway, have a lawyer review your own clause.

title: Fees for Services You Don't Provide
bodyText: No West Virginia statute specifically bars a residential landlord from charging a fee for a service that is not actually provided; the express ban in West Virginia law covers mortgage lenders and brokers. General rules still point the same way. West Virginia's consumer protection act makes unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce unlawful, including representing that services have benefits or characteristics they do not have; whether its private damages action reaches renting a home is not settled. Its debt-collection rules bar a false representation of the character or amount of a claim and, under this library's reading, collecting a charge incidental to the obligation that the lease and a statute do not both authorize; if they apply to rent, a violation can cost actual damages plus a $1,000 penalty per violation. So charge only fees that match a real service or cost, describe each fee accurately in the lease, and stop or refund a recurring service fee when the service ends.

title: Passing Government Fines to a Tenant
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute says whether you may pass a government fine, penalty or nuisance-abatement charge on to a tenant, and none makes a tenant liable to you for one, whatever the lease says. So the lease decides. Where a fine or abatement charge results from a condition or violation that the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest caused by breaking the lease or the law, the library's optional Fines Caused by Tenant clause treats it as the tenant's breach and lets you recover what you actually paid, after written notice with a copy of the citation.

Don't pass on a fine for a condition that is your own duty, such as a code violation from repairs you were required to make. Under this library's reading of West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law, recovering an actual amount the lease makes the tenant's is part of what the tenant agreed to pay, not an add-on fee needing separate authorization; this is not settled. City fees for services such as police, fire and garbage are a separate subject covered in the library's Municipal Service Fees row.

Cities may fine owners under their own ordinances.

title: No Late Fee Cap
bodyText: West Virginia sets no maximum late fee for a residential lease, and no separate late-fee cap for manufactured-home or mobile-home parks. That does not leave the amount open-ended. Specify the fee in the lease and keep it reasonable: the deposit may be applied only to reasonable charges for late payment of rent that the rental agreement specifies. West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law bars collecting a charge incidental to an obligation unless both the agreement and a statute or regulation expressly authorize it, with a penalty of up to $1,000 per violation. This library reads the deposit statute's recognition of reasonable, agreed late charges as that statute, but whether the debt-collection law reaches rent, and how large a fee a court would accept as reasonable, are not settled. A very large fee also risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty. The fixed late-fee limits elsewhere in West Virginia law, such as for storage units and rent-to-own goods, do not apply to renting a home. See the library's Late Fees row for the full rules.

title: No Separate Notice for Nonrefundable Fees
bodyText:
West Virginia does not require a separate notice, a separate document, initials or special type before a fee can be nonrefundable. Its rule is narrower: a pet fee or an application fee stays outside the security deposit law only if you and the tenant expressly agree, in writing, that the fee is nonrefundable. Without that written agreement, a refundable payment that secures the tenant's performance or covers damage is a security deposit, and you must return it with an itemization under the deposit law.

Put the written agreement in the lease for a pet fee, using the library's Nonrefundable Fees clause, and in the signed application for an application fee. The written-agreement rule names only pet fees and application fees. Calling some other payment "nonrefundable" when it in substance secures performance or damage may not take it out of the deposit rules; treat such money as a deposit.

title: Fees for Serving Notices
bodyText: Some leases charge the tenant a fee for preparing, posting or serving a notice, such as a notice of late rent or a notice to quit. No West Virginia statute authorizes, forbids or caps such a fee in a residential lease, and this library does not offer one. The reason is West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law, which by its words reaches anyone collecting a debt from a transaction for personal, family or household purposes. It bars collecting a fee incidental to the debt unless both the agreement and a statute or regulation expressly authorize it, and it bars saying that a debt can be increased by fees that cannot legally be added. A notice fee can be read as a charge added because of a default, and no statute authorizes one for a landlord. A violation can cost actual damages plus a $1,000 penalty per violation. Whether that law reaches rent is not settled. West Virginia also has no general statute voiding contract penalties for leases of homes, so whether a fixed fee is an unenforceable penalty is left to court decisions. If you want a notice fee anyway, add your own clause only after legal advice.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: West Virginia's security deposit law covers every residential rental unit used as a dwelling, and a lease cannot take its protections away. A rental agreement, whether written, electronic or oral, may not contain a term in which the tenant agrees to waive or give up any right or remedy under that law. A term that tries is unenforceable, and if you sue to enforce it, the tenant can recover the actual damages it caused plus reasonable attorney's fees. The protections a lease cannot remove include: return of the deposit with a written itemization by the earlier of 60 days after the tenancy ends or 45 days after a new tenant moves in; the limit of deductions to the uses the law lists; the extra 15 days for an itemization only where damage exceeds the deposit, needs a contractor and you gave written notice in time; the delivery and six-month hold rules; the tenant's right to inspect, or get a copy of, your records of deductions within 72 hours of a written request; the rule that a new owner must return a deposit that is owed; and the tenant's remedy for a willful or bad-faith violation. So don't use terms such as "Tenant waives any itemized statement", "Landlord may keep the deposit for any reason" or "Tenant gives up any claim for damages over the deposit". A charge the lease itself provides for is one of the uses the law allows, so name such charges in the lease. A flat forfeiture of the whole deposit, with no link to rent owed, damage or a charge the lease names, risks being treated as a waiver; avoid it.

title: Setting Deposit Amounts
bodyText: West Virginia does not require you to post, disclose or follow written standards for how you set security deposits, and it has no special rule for landlords who own more than four adjoining units. It does not cap the deposit either. You may set different deposits for different applicants, for example based on rental or credit history, but not because of race, color, religion, ancestry, sex, familial status, blindness, disability or national origin: the West Virginia Fair Housing Act forbids discriminating in the terms or conditions of a rental on those grounds, subject to the Act's limited exemptions. You also may not make an assistance animal requested as a disability accommodation depend on paying a pet fee or deposit. If you vary deposits, the cautious course is to use written criteria applied the same way to every applicant and to keep a record of how each deposit was set.

title: Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: West Virginia has few fixed money limits for a residential lease. Rent: no cap on the amount or on increases, except that during a declared state of emergency or preparedness you may not rent month-to-month housing in the covered area for more than 10 percent above the price 10 days before the declaration, unless your own added costs justify it. Security deposit: no cap and no interest required; a pet fee or application fee counts as part of the deposit unless you and the tenant expressly agree in writing that it is nonrefundable. Application fees, pet fees and pet rent: no cap, but no fee or deposit for an assistance animal a tenant needs because of a disability. Late fee: no cap, but the fee must be reasonable and stated in the lease. Returned check: a fee of up to $25 for a check dishonored for insufficient funds or credit. Unpaid rent: interest as on other contracts. Holdover: no statutory double rent. Attorney fees, collection costs and notice fees: no statute authorizes a landlord to charge them. Under this library's reading of West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law, any charge added because of a default needs both the lease and a statute behind it, with a penalty of up to $1,000 per violation; that reading is not settled. Mishandling a deposit willfully or in bad faith can cost the deposit plus one and a half times the amount wrongfully withheld. Each item has its own row in this library.

title: Collecting Rent for a Unit Needing Repairs
bodyText: No West Virginia statute bars you from demanding or collecting rent because the unit needs repairs, has code violations, or has been condemned or declared unfit, and none requires you to demand the rent before you file to evict for nonpayment. That does not mean the full rent is always owed. If buildings on the property are destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence, the rent is reasonably reduced until you rebuild, unless the lease provides otherwise, and if you do not rebuild as soon as you reasonably can, the tenant may surrender possession and owe no further rent. If the whole property is taken by eminent domain, the rent ends, and a partial taking reduces it in proportion, unless the lease expressly provides otherwise. In an eviction for unpaid rent, the tenant may defend by showing that you breached a material covenant on which the duty to pay rent depends, and the court must hold a hearing on it; your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable is the likeliest such covenant, and what a court would award for its breach turns on case law. So if a unit is unfit, or a city has ordered it vacated, get advice before demanding rent for that time. In an ejectment or unlawful detainer case based on a right of reentry, serving the declaration or starting the action takes the place of the old demand and reentry, but if the lease sets a time before reentry, wait until it has passed.

title: Paying Rent in Installments
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute addresses paying rent in installments, so you and the tenant may agree in the lease that each month's rent is paid in set parts on set dates. Treat each installment as rent due on its own date: an installment that is not paid is unpaid rent, which can support a petition for possession for rent in arrears. No statute says whether installments paid on the lease's schedule are partial payments, and none says whether paying a monthly rent weekly turns a tenancy with no fixed end into a week-to-week tenancy; that would be a question for the courts.

To avoid doubt, keep the rent stated as a monthly amount, say in the lease that the rental period is the month, and give notice to end a month-to-month tenancy by the monthly period. Coordinate your late fee with the schedule: the deposit may cover only reasonable late charges the rental agreement specifies, so say whether a late fee runs from each installment's date or once for the month.

The library's optional Rent Paid in Installments clause allows a late charge only as your late-fee terms allow for the rental period. Whether accepting money outside the schedule waives a default is not settled by statute; see the library's row on accepting rent after a default.

title: Collecting Rent Without the Repair Duty
bodyText: No West Virginia statute says, as the uniform landlord-tenant act does, that a lease, assignment, deed, deed of trust or security instrument cannot let someone collect the rent free of the duty to keep the home fit and habitable. That does not mean the duty can be split off. West Virginia's habitability statute puts the delivery, repair and maintenance duties on the landlord of residential property, and no statute lets a lease or other document waive them. When the property or the landlord's interest is sold, inherited or assigned, the new holder can enforce the lease and collect the rent, and the tenant has the same benefit of the lease's conditions, covenants and promises against the new holder. Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends must also return any deposit owed, regardless of any agreement between you and your successor. No statute says whether a person who only collects the rent, such as a lender or an assignee of rents, also takes on the habitability duties; that would be a question for the courts. So don't set up a lease, management agreement or assignment that sends the rent to one person and leaves the repair duties with no one, and make sure whoever receives the rent can see that repairs are made. If your city has adopted an uninhabitable-property registration under state law, an agent who manages the property or collects its rents counts as an owner for that registration.

title: No Work Card for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires a work card, license or criminal background check for people who work at age-restricted or senior rental housing, or at rental property generally. The state's background-check program covers care providers, such as nursing facilities, home health and hospice agencies, personal care and adult day care providers, and residential care providers that arrange for or provide long-term care services, including assisted living. If your property also provides that kind of care, it is a care business with its own licensing and screening rules; ordinary apartments rented to people 55 or older are not on the list. Housing that qualifies as housing for older persons under the fair housing law may limit occupancy by age without breaking the familial status rules, but that definition sets no staffing requirement. Any screening of employees you choose to do is an employment matter outside this library.

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute deals with a tenant who refuses an inspection in subsidized housing, and no West Virginia statute sets rules for a landlord's entry, so your lease's access terms govern. Federal rules for the Housing Choice Voucher program set the inspection schedule: the housing agency must inspect the unit before the initial lease term, at least every two years during the tenancy (every three years for a small rural agency), and when a family or government official reports a possible deficiency, within 24 hours for a life-threatening one and 15 days for others.

The family must allow the agency to inspect at reasonable times after reasonable notice; that is a program obligation the agency enforces, not a ground the federal rules give you. During the lease term you may end a voucher tenancy only for a serious or repeated lease violation, a violation of law tied to the tenant's use of the home, or other good cause, so if you want a tenant's refusal of a program inspection to count as a breach of the lease, the lease must say so; this library offers an optional clause that does. The agency may not charge the family for an inspection. It may charge you a reasonable fee for a reinspection that shows a deficiency you were responsible for was not corrected, and you may not pass that fee on to the family.

West Virginia's fair housing law makes it unlawful to tell someone that a dwelling is not available for inspection, sale or rental when it is, because of a protected trait; source of income is not one of those traits under state law, but check local ordinances before treating voucher holders differently.

title: Subsidized Rent When a Unit Fails Standards
bodyText: No West Virginia statute reduces rent because part of a unit is uninhabitable, and none says how a rent reduction is split between the tenant's share and a housing subsidy. The only state rule that reduces rent for the unit's condition is the casualty rule: if buildings are destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence, the rent is reasonably reduced until you rebuild, unless the lease provides otherwise. No statute says whether that reduction comes off the subsidy, the tenant's share or both, so talk to the housing agency before you change either. Federal rules for the Housing Choice Voucher program apply when an agency inspection finds deficiencies and notifies you in writing. You must correct a life-threatening deficiency within 24 hours and others within 30 days, or any extension the agency approves. The agency may withhold its payments once it has notified you; if you fix the problem in time, it resumes them and pays for the withheld period, but if you don't, it must abate its payments and will not pay for the abated period, and it must end the payment contract if the unit still fails 60 days after the abatement notice, or any longer period it sets. The tenant is not responsible for the agency's share, so you can't collect the withheld or abated amount from the tenant, and you may not end the tenancy because assistance was withheld or abated; the tenant may end the tenancy during an abatement. If the agency finds the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the deficiency beyond ordinary use, it may waive your responsibility to fix it, and then it may not withhold or abate the payment. These rules apply to payment contracts signed or renewed on or after June 6, 2024; older contracts follow the earlier version.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule says anything special about late fees when a housing subsidy pays part of the rent, so the general rule applies: a late fee must be reasonable and specified in the lease. Federal rules for the Housing Choice Voucher program do set limits. The tenant is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing agency pays, the agency's failure to pay is not a lease violation by the tenant, and during the lease term you may not end the tenancy because the agency did not pay. You may not demand or accept more from the tenant than the tenant's share, and you must return any excess. Whether you can collect a penalty from the agency for a late assistance payment depends on the payment contract, which provides for one only if such penalties follow local practice and law, you charge them to assisted and unassisted tenants alike, and you also charge the tenant for paying its own share late. The federal tenancy addendum overrides any conflicting lease term. So figure any late fee only on the tenant's own share, never charge the tenant because the agency paid late, and follow your payment contract for agency delays.

title: Passing On Property Tax and Insurance Increases
bodyText:
One West Virginia statute bears on passing taxes to a tenant, and none forbids it: a tenant's promise in a lease "to pay the taxes" covers all taxes, levies and assessments on the property, but not an assessment for a permanent local improvement, such as paving a street or sidewalk, or a tax on your rental income from the property, unless the lease expressly says so (see the optional Special District Fees and Assessments clause). No West Virginia statute addresses passing tax or insurance increases to a residential tenant as such, or passing insurance costs at all. Without such a term, the rent you agreed on stands and those costs stay yours.

If you want the tenant to share an increase, the lease must say so: state the tenant's share as a fixed percentage of the increase over a stated base year, show the bill and your calculation, and credit the tenant's share of any later reduction or refund. The library's optional Tax and Insurance Increases clause does this. At the end of the tenancy a security deposit may be applied only to the uses the deposit law lists, which include rent due and other charges the rental agreement provides for, so an unpaid share can come out of the deposit only if the lease provides for it.

The consumer debt-collection law can be read as allowing a share the lease assigns, because it is part of what the tenant agreed to pay, but don't pass on penalties or interest caused by your own late payment of a tax bill or premium; whether that law reaches rent is for the courts. During a declared state of emergency or state of preparedness, the price of a month-to-month rental may not rise more than 10 percent above its level 10 days before the declaration unless the increase comes from certain added supplier, labor or materials costs; a tax or insurance increase is not clearly one of them, so don't bill a new share on a month-to-month tenancy during an emergency if it would push the total over that line.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law
bodyText: West Virginia has no truth-in-renting law. No statute or rule requires you to give a residential tenant a state statement of tenant rights, to put a truth-in-renting notice in the lease, or makes it a violation in itself to offer a lease that contains a forbidden term. Other rules do similar work. A lease term in which the tenant gives up rights under the security deposit law is unenforceable, and if you sue to enforce one, the tenant can recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. A residential lease must be written in clear, everyday language, readable type and organized sections, and a tenant who asks can have it rewritten. Several other terms are void, and this library reads the consumer debt-collection law to bar collecting default charges that no statute authorizes. Leave void terms out of your lease rather than relying on a court to strike them; the library's rows on prohibited lease terms and plain language list them.

title: Charging Separately for Parking
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to rent parking separately from the home, or to include it, and none regulates a separate parking charge. You may include parking in the rent or offer it as an add-on for a separate monthly charge, but say which in the lease. A parking charge the lease sets is money owed under the rental agreement, so this library treats it as rent: it can be taken from the deposit at the end of the tenancy like other unpaid rent, and the library's optional parking clause says so.

Keep the charge the same during a fixed term unless the lease lets you change it, and don't add a late fee to it unless the lease's late-fee terms cover it. If a tenant with a disability asks for an accessible or assigned space as an accommodation, handle it under the fair housing rules rather than the parking charge. Under a State Tax Department rule, parking spaces rented for more than 30 consecutive days are not subject to sales tax, while parking offered to the public for a fee generally is; ask the Tax Department if you rent parking by the day or week or to people who are not your tenants.

Local zoning may require a number of parking spaces for a building; check your city or county.

title: Utility Allowances With a Tenant-Paid Overage
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule caps what you may charge a tenant for a utility you bill back or limits a utility allowance with a tenant-paid overage. Paying a utility up to a set monthly allowance and having the tenant reimburse the excess is a lease term no statute forbids, but it works only if the lease says so, and for water or electricity it is subject to the Commission's resale rules described below, and at the end of the tenancy you may apply the deposit only to unpaid utilities that you were billed for and paid and that the lease makes the tenant's obligation. This library does not offer a separate allowance clause. Its Utility Billing clause already covers utilities you bill to the tenant, and the common allowance clause used in other states says the overage is not rent, which in West Virginia would give up remedies you otherwise have, because the deposit law counts nearly all money owed under the lease as rent. The Public Service Commission's rules bar a utility customer from reselling water unless the customer is itself a public utility, and bar a utility from furnishing electricity to a customer for resale; its electric rule also says apartment buildings and other multi-unit residential dwellings should be individually metered unless an exemption is shown. Whether billing tenants for water or electricity by submeter, by formula or as an overage counts as resale depends on Commission decisions, so the cautious course is to include water and electricity in the rent or have tenants take service in their own names. If you want an allowance arrangement, you may add your own clause with legal advice: state the allowance, which utilities it covers, how you will show the actual bill, and when the excess is due.

title: No Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: West Virginia has no program that pays a landlord, or gives a tax credit, for renting to a veteran, and no statute regulates a rent discount for veterans. The state's veterans' housing programs help veterans buy a home through the Housing Development Fund, and the state's veterans tax credit goes to employers who hire certain veterans, not to landlords. Veteran or military status is not one of the traits West Virginia's fair housing law protects, but federal law gives servicemembers lease rights, such as ending a lease after entering military service or receiving qualifying orders, and protection for them and their dependents from eviction during military service except by court order where the rent is under a federal ceiling; see the library's servicemember row. If you choose to offer a veterans' discount, write it into the lease, state who qualifies and what proof you accept, and offer it on the same terms to everyone who qualifies. Federal programs such as HUD-VASH vouchers for veterans are run by local housing agencies under their own rules.

title: Winter Absences and Frozen Pipes
bodyText:
Some states make a tenant warn the landlord before moving out or leaving a unit empty in winter, so the pipes can be protected. West Virginia has no such rule: no statute or agency rule requires a tenant to give notice before vacating, or before leaving the home empty, in cold weather. What West Virginia does say runs the other way: for a unit on direct public utility connections, you must supply running water and reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April, unless the unit is built so that heat or hot water comes from an installation under the tenant's exclusive control.

Any winter notice duty therefore has to come from the lease. This library's lease asks the tenant to tell you, by its first day, of any absence of more than 7 days, and offers an optional cold-weather clause asking for advance notice of a winter absence or move-out and, where the tenant controls the heat, that the heat stay on at a set minimum while the tenant is away. A lease promise from you to do more than the statute requires binds you, so do not promise in the lease to winterize or check an empty unit unless you will. If a tenant who owes rent has abandoned the property, use the posted one-month notice before you take possession.

title: Eviction Fees and Penalty Clauses
bodyText: Some states void any lease clause that charges the tenant a penalty because an eviction notice was served or an eviction case was filed. West Virginia has no such ban, but it has no statute authorizing such a charge either, and this library does not offer one. The reason is West Virginia's consumer debt-collection law, which bars collecting a fee or charge incidental to a debt unless both the agreement and a statute or regulation expressly authorize it, and bars representing that a debt may be increased by fees that cannot legally be added; a violation can cost the tenant's actual damages plus a $1,000 penalty per violation. An eviction fee or penalty can be read as a charge added because of a default, and no statute authorizes one for a landlord. Whether that law reaches rent is not settled. West Virginia also has no general statute voiding contract penalties or unreasonable liquidated damages in leases of homes; the Uniform Commercial Code's rules on liquidated damages cover sales and leases of goods, so whether a fixed eviction charge is an unenforceable penalty is left to case law. What you can recover is set by the court: in the eviction case you may claim all rent due and owing, and the court may award the costs it allows; in an unlawful detainer case you may also claim damages for the detention and any waste. Actual losses, such as damage beyond normal wear and tear, are handled under the security deposit law and the lease's damage terms. If you want an eviction charge anyway, add your own clause only after legal advice.

title: Who Can Be Served With Eviction Papers
bodyText: In a West Virginia summary eviction, you must have notice of the hearing served on the tenant right after the court sets the hearing date, either under the civil rules for serving a summons or by certified mail, return receipt requested; you then file the petition with the proof of service or the signed return receipt. Under the civil rule, papers may be handed to the tenant, left at the tenant's home with someone 18 or older who lives there, delivered by the sheriff, or sent by the clerk by certified or first-class mail, and anyone 18 or older who is not a party may serve them, so you cannot serve them yourself. Serve every tenant you name in the petition. The rule also allows delivery to an agent or attorney-in-fact the person has authorized by appointment to receive court papers. No West Virginia statute or court rule says whether a lease can make that appointment, and this library does not offer a clause naming someone to accept eviction papers for the tenant: whether a lease term counts as such an appointment, especially one naming your own agent, is a question of case law; if a court rejects the appointment, the service and any default judgment can fall; and the magistrate court rules give a defendant served through an agent 30 days to answer in ordinary cases, which may not fit a five-day eviction schedule. If you want such a clause anyway, add your own only after legal advice, and still serve the tenant directly. If a tenant shows you a card from the Secretary of State's Address Confidentiality Program, which protects survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking, the Secretary of State is the participant's agent for service of court papers: you may serve two copies on the Secretary of State's office by mail or delivery, and the office forwards them by certified mail. Courts accept the participant's substitute address for new public records unless the Secretary of State decides otherwise, so ask the magistrate clerk how to describe the property in the petition and get advice before filing.

title: Relief From Forfeiture for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: West Virginia lets a tenant undo a forfeiture for unpaid rent by paying. In an ejectment or unlawful detainer case to recover the property because rent is in arrears, the case must stop if, before trial, the tenant or anyone else with a claim to the property pays or tenders to you or your attorney, or pays into court, all the rent and arrears with interest and costs. After a judgment for possession is carried out, the tenant still has twelve months to pay the rent in arrears with interest and costs, or to sue in equity for relief, before losing all right to be restored, and a mortgagee or trustee of the tenant's interest has the same right. Where you took possession after an abandonment under the posted one-month notice and chose to keep the tenant liable while you relet, the tenant may take the property back by paying all arrears and other lease liabilities and giving you written notice, unless you have already relet it. Whether the pay-before-trial rule also applies to a summary eviction petition is not settled by statute, though a tenant there may raise any defense available in ejectment or unlawful detainer. If a tenant offers everything owed, with interest and costs, before the hearing, get legal advice before refusing it. The full rules are in the row on paying the rent to stop an eviction, and this library's default clause does not limit the tenant's right.

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Notice
bodyText: Some states with good-cause eviction laws require a landlord to tell tenants in writing whether the law covers their unit, and to state the reason when a lease is not renewed. West Virginia has no good-cause eviction law for residential rentals, so there is no such notice to give: you may let a fixed-term lease end on its last day without notice or a reason, and end a periodic tenancy with the required notice without stating a reason (see the rows on just cause and on notice to end a tenancy). On a property covered by the federal CARES Act, give at least 30 days' written notice to vacate before you require the tenant to leave (see "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties"). West Virginia's good-cause rules apply only to rentals of sites for factory-built (manufactured) homes, which have their own rules. Two limits still apply. Federal fair housing law and the state fair housing act bar ending or refusing to renew a tenancy for a discriminatory reason. And if the tenant has a Housing Choice Voucher, during the lease term you may end the tenancy only on the federal grounds, and you must give the tenant a written notice specifying the grounds at or before the start of the eviction case, with a copy of any eviction notice to the housing agency (see the voucher row).

title: Your Remedies When a Tenant Defaults
bodyText: When a tenant defaults, West Virginia gives you remedies for possession and for money, and you can pursue them together. Possession comes only through the courts: a summary eviction petition in magistrate court or circuit court for unpaid rent, a lease breach or damage, or an unlawful detainer case for a tenant who stays after the right to possession has ended. In any trial involving possession of rental property you may also claim and get judgment for all rent due and owing, and if the tenant files no answer the court may include the unpaid rent in its possession order. In an unlawful detainer case you may also recover the value of the use of the property for up to three years before you sued, plus damage or waste, if you file a statement of them with the summons. You may also sue for money alone: rent of every kind may be recovered by a lawsuit, and you may sue for a reasonable payment for use and occupation of the property, with interest as on other contracts. The rent statute does not require you to end the tenancy before suing for rent already due. Magistrate court hears civil claims of up to $20,000, not counting interest and costs; larger claims go to circuit court, and in an eviction or unlawful detainer case involving $2,500 or more any party may move the case to circuit court by paying the filing fee. West Virginia has no separate small-claims court; magistrate court is the court for smaller claims. For rent after the tenancy ends: if a tenant abandons owing rent, you can keep the tenant liable for the rest of the term for the shortfall on reletting by saying in your posted notice that you will relet; in other cases, whether rent for the rest of the term can be recovered after the tenancy ends is a question of case law. Other tools are distress for rent through the sheriff and applying the security deposit as the deposit law allows. Deadlines: an unlawful detainer case within three years, distress within one year after the rent falls due, and a suit on a written lease the tenant signed generally within ten years (five years on an oral lease). This library's lease does not ask the tenant to pay your attorney fees.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Some states let a lease give the landlord a right to change the locks on a tenant who is behind on rent, with advance notice and a key on request. West Virginia has no such right: no statute or court rule allows a residential landlord to lock out a tenant, change the locks, remove doors or cut off utilities because rent is unpaid, and this library offers no lockout clause. A lease term cannot create the right either, because the lawful ways to recover possession are a court eviction carried out by the sheriff or, for a tenant who abandons owing rent, the posted one-month notice. A tenant who is forcibly or unlawfully turned out of possession may sue within three years to get the property back, without proving title, and recover damages for the time kept out. For units on direct public utility connections you must also supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April, unless the tenant controls the installation. The only statute that spells out a ban on lockouts and utility shutoffs is written for rentals of sites for factory-built homes; for ordinary rentals, follow the court process. What else a lockout may expose you to is a question of case law. See the row on lockouts and utility shutoffs.

title: Shortening or Waiving the Notice to End a Tenancy
bodyText:
West Virginia lets the lease change the notice needed to end a periodic tenancy. The statutory notice, three months before the end of a year for a year-to-year tenancy and one full rental period for a month-to-month or other shorter tenancy, does not apply where, by special agreement, the lease fixes a different notice period or provides that no notice is to be given. This library offers an optional clause that uses this rule to set a shorter notice period, for both you and the tenant, no longer than the period the law would otherwise require. It does not offer a clause waiving notice altogether, although the statute allows one: with no notice, either side could end the tenancy without any warning, so the tenant could leave owing you a vacancy and you could face an immediate move-out, and a court reading a no-notice term against the party who wrote it is a risk; whether courts enforce such a term in a residential lease is case law.

If you want a no-notice term anyway, add your own clause only after legal advice. Some notices cannot be waived by the lease. A fixed-term lease needs no notice to end on its last day, and no statute requires a notice before you file to evict for unpaid rent, but if the property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, federal law bars requiring the tenant to vacate until 30 days after a notice to vacate (see the CARES Act row), and a voucher tenancy needs a written notice of the grounds (see the voucher row).

A lease term requiring a longer notice than the statute provides risks being void, and a deceased tenant's estate's right to end the lease on notice cannot be waived. Give every notice in writing and keep proof of delivery.

title: Move-Out Notice Forms and Work During a Notice
bodyText: Some states require a warning on any move-out form you ask a tenant to sign if it adds terms not in the lease, or bar work that makes a unit unlivable while a notice to vacate is running. West Virginia has neither rule in general: no statute or agency rule governs what a tenant's notice to vacate form may contain, and none bars alterations during the notice period. A tenant's notice to end a periodic tenancy simply has to give the required time and may be served on you or your agent; it needs no form of yours. If you hand tenants a move-out form, keep it to the move-out date and contact details and do not slip in new obligations, such as cleaning fees or a waiver of rights; whether a tenant who signs such a form is bound by terms not in the lease is a question of case law, and new charges also run into the state's consumer debt-collection limits. Two rules do reach the notice period. If you convert the building to a condominium, cooperative or other common-interest community, each residential tenant gets at least 120 days' notice, and the terms of the tenancy may not be altered during that period. And until the tenancy ends you must keep the unit fit and habitable and in repair, so work that leaves an occupied unit without water, heat, sanitation or other essentials, or out of line with the housing and safety codes, can breach that duty and give the tenant a defense in any eviction for unpaid rent. Schedule disruptive work for after the tenant leaves.

title: Ending a Lease So You or Family Can Move In
bodyText:
West Virginia has no owner move-in law: no statute gives you a right to end a tenancy so that you or a relative can live in the unit, and none limits that reason or requires the unit to stay owner-occupied for a set time afterward. Because West Virginia has no just-cause rule, you usually do not need one. A fixed-term lease ends on its last day with no notice required, and a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy can be ended for any lawful reason with the required notice.

What you cannot do without a lease term is end a fixed-term lease early because you want to move in. If you may need that, choose this library's optional Owner Occupancy clause before signing: it lets you end a fixed term early for your own or a named family member's occupancy on written notice of at least 30 days, ending on the last day of a rental month, with rent owed only through that date. If you leave the clause out, you have no such right until the term ends. If the tenant stays past the termination date, recover possession only through the court.

Two federal limits: for a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, during the initial lease term you may not end the tenancy because you want to use the unit for yourself or your family, and on a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal program you may not require the tenant to vacate until 30 days after a notice to vacate. Fair housing law applies to the choice of which tenancy to end.

title: No Possession Bond for Tenants
bodyText: Some states let a landlord take a bond from the tenant, often with a confessed judgment, promising to give up possession when the lease ends. West Virginia has no such possession bond: no statute or court rule provides a bond a residential tenant gives to guarantee moving out, or a judgment for possession the tenant confesses in advance. At the end of a fixed term no notice is needed under state law, and if the tenant stays you recover possession through the court. On a property covered by the federal CARES Act, give at least 30 days' written notice to vacate before you require the tenant to leave (see "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties"). The bonds and payments that do arise in an eviction are court-procedure ones. A party who appeals a magistrate court judgment to circuit court must post an appeal bond, which the magistrate court rules set at not less than the judgment plus the reasonable costs of the appeal (the statute sets a range from the appeal costs up to that sum), unless the party is allowed to proceed without paying costs; a tenant who is granted a continuance of the eviction hearing must pay into court the rent that comes due during it; and a landlord who seeks an attachment because a tenant is removing belongings must give a bond. Once a case is filed, a tenant may confess judgment in court, and the magistrate enters it in writing. A confession-of-judgment clause written into the lease is a different thing: see the confession-of-judgment row, and do not use one. Secure the tenant's obligations with the security deposit and, if needed, a written guaranty instead.

title: Late Benefit Checks and Eviction
bodyText: Some states make a court postpone a nonpayment eviction, or reinstate the tenancy, when the tenant shows that a Social Security, disability, public assistance or housing voucher payment was late. West Virginia has no such rule: no statute or court rule gives a tenant a defense, a continuance or reinstatement because a benefit payment was delayed. In a summary eviction, the court may continue the hearing only for cause, never as of right, and a tenant who gets a continuance must pay into court the rent that comes due during it. A tenant in an ejectment or unlawful detainer case for unpaid rent can stop the case by paying all the rent and arrears with interest and costs before trial, and whether that rule also reaches a summary eviction is not settled by statute (see the row on paying the rent to stop an eviction). Federal law adds one rule for Housing Choice Voucher tenancies: the tenant owes only the family's share of the rent, and you may not end the tenancy during the lease term because the housing agency failed to pay its share (see the voucher row). If a tenant tells you a benefit check is late, accepting a short payment plan in writing is often cheaper than filing.

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: West Virginia law says nothing specific about a tenant's bankruptcy: no state statute or court rule says whether an eviction, or the sheriff's removal under a possession order, goes ahead once you learn the tenant has filed. Federal bankruptcy law controls. A bankruptcy petition automatically stops most acts against the tenant, including starting or continuing an eviction case, enforcing a judgment and any act to obtain possession of the tenant's estate property, which can include the lease. Two exceptions matter to residential landlords. First, if you obtained a judgment for possession before the tenant filed, the stay generally does not stop you from completing the eviction; but if the tenant files a certification under penalty of perjury that state law would let them cure the whole rent default after the judgment and deposits the next 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy clerk, the stay holds for 30 days, and if they then certify that they have cured the whole default, the stay keeps protecting them unless the bankruptcy court orders otherwise on your objection. Whether West Virginia law allows a cure after a summary eviction judgment is not settled: a tenant in an ejectment or unlawful detainer case for unpaid rent may pay the rent in arrears with interest and costs within twelve months after the judgment is carried out, and whether that reaches a summary eviction is case law. Second, an eviction based on endangerment of the property or illegal drug use there can proceed 15 days after you file and serve a sworn certification with the bankruptcy court, unless the tenant objects and shows the problem did not exist or has been fixed. Otherwise you need the bankruptcy court's permission (relief from the stay) before you file or continue an eviction. In a chapter 7 case, a residential lease the trustee does not assume within 60 days after the order for relief, unless the court extends that time, is treated as rejected; in chapters 11, 12 and 13 the decision can wait until a plan is confirmed. A lease term that ends the lease just because the tenant files for bankruptcy or is insolvent is generally unenforceable once the case starts. A willful violation of the stay can cost you the tenant's actual damages, costs and attorney fees, and sometimes punitive damages. If you get notice of a filing, stop collection and eviction steps and get advice before acting.

title: Barring Non-Tenants From the Property
bodyText: West Virginia's criminal trespass law lets you keep an unwanted non-tenant, such as a former tenant who has moved out, a person who caused trouble, or someone with no business there, off the parts of your property you control. A person who knowingly enters a building, or the yard and grounds around it, without being authorized, licensed or invited commits trespass, and so does a person who was allowed in but refuses to leave after the owner, the tenant, or an agent of either asks them to; it is a misdemeanor. For outdoor areas apart from a building, entering or staying is trespass if the person was told not to, or the land is posted, fenced or cultivated; a person who defies a leave order personally given by the owner, the tenant or an agent faces a higher penalty. Posting means signs saying no trespassing in letters at least two inches high no more than 500 feet apart along the boundary and at each entrance, or the purple paint marks the statute describes. Entry with permission, spoken or written, is not trespass unless signs prohibit it, nor is entry by government officers acting under law or by a utility using its easement. A trespasser who damages property owes you twice the damage, including cleanup. Practical steps: give the person a written notice, dated and signed by you or your manager, naming them and the areas they may not enter, keep a copy, and call the police if they return. Be careful with a tenant's own guests: the statute lets the tenant authorize entry and ask people to leave too, and it does not say whose word controls when you and your tenant disagree about a visitor; that is case law, so bar a tenant's guest only from common areas, for a concrete reason, and with advice. Do not use trespass to remove a tenant or former tenant who is still living there; that takes a court eviction, and police squatter removal does not apply to current or former lawful tenants. Fair housing law applies to whom you bar.

title: Which Casualty and Re-Renting Rules a Lease Can Change
bodyText:
West Virginia lets a lease change some of its casualty rules and is silent on the rest. If a building you own on the property is destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence, the tenant gets a reasonable rent reduction until it is replaced, unless the lease provides otherwise, so the lease may change that reduction. The library's Fire or Casualty Damage clause does so in a measured way: rent drops in proportion to the part the tenant cannot use, and not at all if the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent caused the damage by fault or negligence.

If you do not rebuild as soon as you reasonably can, the tenant may move out and owe no further rent. The statute does not say whether a lease can remove that right, so the library keeps it, and you should not rely on a lease term that takes it away. A tenant's promise to leave the property in good repair does not make a tenant who was not at fault rebuild or pay for buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise, unless other words in the lease show that the parties meant the tenant to be bound.

The library does not offer such words: they would put the cost of rebuilding on a residential tenant, and your duty to keep the home fit and habitable cannot safely be shifted by the lease. If you want them anyway, add your own clause only after legal advice. If the whole property is taken by eminent domain, rent ends, and a partial taking reduces it, unless the lease expressly provides otherwise; the library leaves those rules in place.

Re-renting is different. If a tenant who owes rent abandons the property, the law requires a posted notice giving one month to pay before you take possession, and lets you choose to add a notice that you will re-rent and hold the tenant liable for any shortfall in rent. Those are statutory steps, and no statute lets a lease change them. No statute says whether you must otherwise try to re-rent to reduce your loss, or whether a lease can excuse you; the library's default clause promises reasonable efforts to the extent the law requires and offers no clause waiving them, and making and documenting reasonable efforts to re-rent is the safe course.

title: No Emergency Contact Rule
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour telephone number, to put a management website or social-services hotline notice in the lease, or to keep a list of tenants' emergency contacts, and none limits asking a tenant for one. Giving tenants a number to call about urgent repairs is still good practice, because it helps you hear about leaks, fires and other damage quickly.

If you want a person to call when you cannot reach the tenant in an emergency, the library offers an optional clause in which the tenant names an emergency contact, you agree to use the contact only for emergencies and urgent conditions at the property, and the lease makes clear that the contact owes no rent, is not the tenant's agent and has no right to enter. A person who agrees to answer for the tenant's rent must sign a written guaranty; naming an emergency contact is not one.

West Virginia has no general statute limiting what a landlord may disclose about tenants, so keep the contact's details private and use them only as the clause says.

title: Ending a Lease After an Environmental Event
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule gives you, or the tenant, a right to end a residential lease because of an environmental or public-health event, such as contamination, a chemical spill, a utility-system failure or a government order to vacate. The one event rule belongs to the tenant: if a building you own on the property is destroyed or damaged by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence, rent is reasonably reduced unless the lease provides otherwise, and if you do not rebuild as soon as you reasonably can, the tenant may move out and owe no further rent (see the Fire or Casualty Damage clause).

Some events also put duties on you. If law enforcement notifies you that a clandestine drug laboratory was found on the property, you must keep the property unoccupied and secured until the Department of Health certifies the remediation, or demolish it, and you must disclose the laboratory to any potential occupant (see the drug laboratory row). Cities and counties may order unfit dwellings vacated and closed (see the condemned premises row).

Because the law gives you no exit of your own, the library offers an optional clause that lets either you or the tenant end the lease by written notice when a government order, or a legal duty to keep the property empty, results from an environmental or public-health condition you did not cause by failing to meet your obligations; rent stops on the termination date, prepaid rent is refunded and the deposit is handled as the deposit rules require. You still recover possession only through the court process, and a tenant who caused the condition stays liable for the damage.

title: No Inspection Notice or Penalty
bodyText: West Virginia does not require you to offer the tenant a move-in or move-out inspection, or to tell the tenant of a right to attend one, so there is no penalty or loss of the deposit for leaving such a notice out. No West Virginia statute sets a notice period for entering to inspect during the tenancy either, so there is no statutory penalty for inspecting without notice; your entry rights and notice come from the lease (see the entry rows). Two deposit rules do matter. You must keep an itemized record of every deduction from each tenant's deposit for one year after the tenancy ends, and let the tenant or the tenant's agent or attorney inspect it during normal business hours within 72 hours of a written request, or give them a copy within that time. And if you fail to follow any part of the deposit law willfully or not in good faith, the tenant can recover the unreturned deposit plus one and a half times the amount wrongfully withheld (see the deposit penalty row). Because deductions for damage are reduced by reasonable wear and tear, a dated move-in and move-out record of the property's condition, with photos, is still the best way to support what you keep.

title: No Initials Requirement for Lease Terms
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires a residential tenant to initial a lease term, such as a notice period for ending the tenancy, or to sign one separately, and none makes a term unenforceable because it was not initialed. Asking the tenant to initial key terms can still help you show that the tenant saw them. The rule that matters for notice terms is different: a lease provision requiring a longer notice period than West Virginia's termination statutes provide risks being void and unenforceable, whether or not the tenant initials it, so the library's optional Termination Notice clause lets you set a notice period no longer than the one the law would otherwise require. The initials rules that do appear in West Virginia law are for self-storage rental agreements.

title: Fixed Damages for a Tenant's Breach
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule permits, forbids or limits a fixed amount of damages (liquidated damages) or a penalty for a tenant's breach of a residential lease, and West Virginia has no general contract statute, like some states have, voiding damages fixed in advance. The statutes that use those words are written for other contracts: the commercial code lets a contract for the sale of goods, or a lease of goods, set damages in advance only at a reasonable amount, and voids an unreasonably large amount as a penalty, but a lease of a home is not a sale or lease of goods.

Whether a fixed charge for a breach of a residential lease is an enforceable estimate of your loss or an unenforceable penalty is a question of case law. There is a second risk. Under this library's reading of the Consumer Credit and Protection Act, which courts have not settled, a charge imposed because the tenant defaulted may be collected only if both the lease and a statute authorize it, and no statute authorizes a fixed damages charge for a breach; collecting a charge the law does not allow may be a prohibited debt collection practice.

A price the tenant chooses to pay for an option, such as a fee to end the lease early, is different: it is part of what the tenant agreed to pay. So the library offers no liquidated-damages clause. A tenant who wants to leave a fixed-term lease early can use the Early Termination clause, which ends the lease on notice and a fee; a tenant who simply leaves owes the rent and actual damages the abandonment and re-renting rules and the default clause allow, not a preset sum.

If you want a fixed-damages term anyway, add your own clause only after legal advice.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule sets rules for entering a rented home to provide regularly scheduled services, such as changing furnace or air-conditioning filters, pest treatment or checking smoke detectors, and none allows entry without notice for those services just because the lease says so conspicuously. Because West Virginia has no entry statute at all, your right to enter comes from the lease.

The library's entry clause gives you reasonable access during normal business hours on at least 24 hours' notice, except in an emergency. If you want a fixed service schedule, use the optional scheduled-services clause: it lists the services and how often they happen, sets the hours, and has you give advance notice of each visit and knock before entering. Keep a real notice and reasonable hours, because the tenant's right to possession is defined by case law.

Some services are yours by statute: you must provide, install and replace the smoke detectors required in one- and two-family dwellings, while the tenant must do routine maintenance on them, so a scheduled check is a sensible item for the list. If a tenant refuses an entry the lease allows, document your request and the refusal; a breach of a lease covenant is a ground for a summary eviction case.

title: No Pets-and-Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule makes you give a tenant a state fact sheet or any other information about pets and eviction, at signing or later, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat. West Virginia also has no special eviction steps for a household with animals. After a court grants you possession, the rules for belongings the tenant leaves behind cover personal property in general and say nothing about animals (see the post-eviction property row). A live animal cannot safely be stored or thrown out like furniture, so the cautious course is to tell the tenant in writing, before the move-out date the court sets, that every animal must go with them. If an animal is left behind anyway, report it to a humane officer or your local animal control agency rather than keeping, giving away or disposing of it yourself. Any person may report an animal believed to be abandoned or neglected to a humane officer and is not liable, civilly or criminally, for making the report, and the humane officer takes possession of an animal believed to be abandoned. Separately, you may not evict a tenant with a disability because they need a guide animal, and a no-pets policy does not apply to that animal (see the assistance animal rows). Your own pet rules are in the pet clause.

title: Shorter Notice for Showings
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule sets how much notice you must give before showing a rented home to prospective tenants or buyers, so there is no statutory notice for a tenant to waive, and no rule that a shorter-notice agreement must be in a separate signed document. The notice for showings is whatever the lease says. The library's entry clause promises at least 24 hours' notice, except in an emergency, during normal business hours.

If you want to show the home on shorter notice near the end of the tenancy, use the optional showings clause, which sets the shorter notice and the hours for showings in the last part of the term or after either side gives notice to end the tenancy, and leaves every other entry under the regular entry clause. Whatever you choose, keep the notice real and the hours reasonable: the tenant has a right to possession that only case law defines. If a tenant refuses an entry the lease allows, document your request and the refusal; a breach of a lease covenant is a ground for a summary eviction case.

title: No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Exemption Notice
bodyText: West Virginia has no statewide rent cap and no just-cause eviction rule for ordinary residential rentals, so there is nothing to be exempt from and no exemption notice to put in a lease. You may raise rent and end a periodic tenancy on proper notice without stating a reason (see the rent control and no for-cause eviction rows). The only statewide limit on rent is temporary: during a declared state of emergency or state of preparedness, rent on a month-to-month rental in the affected area may not rise more than 10 percent above the price 10 days before the declaration, unless the increase comes directly from added costs (see the disaster rent limits row); that rule requires no notice to the tenant. The good-cause termination rules in West Virginia law apply only to rented factory-built home sites. Check your city's ordinances.

title: No Tenant Protection Notice or Purchase Right
bodyText: West Virginia has no statewide rent cap or just-cause eviction law for ordinary residential rentals, so no lease notice telling the tenant that one applies (see the rent-cap exemption row). West Virginia also gives tenants no general right of first refusal or opportunity to buy when you sell a rental property, and requires no notice to tenants of a planned sale. The one exception is a conversion: if you convert a residential rental building into a condominium, cooperative or other common interest community, you must give each residential tenant in possession notice of the conversion and the public offering statement at least 120 days before they must leave, and for 60 days after that notice you must offer to sell each residential unit to the tenant who leases it; if the tenant does not buy, for the next 180 days you may not offer that unit to anyone else on a better price or terms (see the condominium conversion row). Check your city's ordinances.

title: No Repeal Date on West Virginia Tenant Laws
bodyText: West Virginia's landlord-tenant statutes, including the rules on ending tenancies, security deposits and summary eviction, the fair housing act and the emergency rent limit, have no built-in expiration or repeal date, and West Virginia has no rent-cap or just-cause law that could expire. Some agency rules that reach rentals do carry end dates, after which they stop having effect unless the agency renews them: the Human Rights Commission's rule on disability discrimination, including in housing, and its rule on assistance animals in housing are set to end on August 1, 2030, and the Department of Health's rule on cleaning up former clandestine drug laboratories, including an owner's duty to keep the property unoccupied and to disclose the laboratory to a potential occupant, is set to end on August 1, 2027. The fair housing and drug laboratory statutes behind those rules stay in force either way. Check for a renewed rule after those dates.

title: Agreeing How Notices Are Given
bodyText:
West Virginia's landlord-tenant statutes do not use an actual-notice standard, and none lets you and the tenant agree on an extra way to give a notice the law requires. Each statute sets its own method: a written notice to end a periodic tenancy, posting and mailing for abandoned property, personal delivery or mail for the deposit refund and itemization, and service under the court rules or certified mail for an eviction hearing (see "Delivering Notices"). No residential rule turns on actual notice to you or to your rent agent.

What you can agree on is electronic dealing. The electronic transactions act applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, and either one may later refuse to do so; that right cannot be waived. If you have agreed and a law requires information to be given in writing, an email or other electronic record counts only if the tenant can print or store it when it arrives. Where a law requires posting, mail or another specific method, you must still use that method.

Notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of the tenant's primary residence are outside the act's electronic-records rules (its article 1), so give those on paper by the method the law or your lease sets. An electronic record counts as received when it reaches the email address or system the recipient designated or uses, even if no one reads it, but if you know it did not arrive, send it again another way.
