The optional clause "Email and Text Delivery of Routine Notices" records the tenant's agreement to email and text delivery of routine notices that no law governs, such as notice that you plan to enter, and keeps paper for everything else.

title: Other Rules West Virginia Does and Does Not Have
bodyText: Several rules found in other states are missing in West Virginia, and one is present. (1) False rental applications: no statute gives you a special right to end a lease because the application was false. The library's Accuracy of Rental Application clause makes a material falsehood a breach of the lease, which you can enforce through the summary eviction for breach of a leasehold covenant; any fraud remedy beyond that is case law. (2) Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors: West Virginia does have a shield. A violation of the detector statute may not be treated as evidence of negligence, contributory negligence or comparative negligence in a civil damages case, and may not be a defense in any civil case involving an insurance policy, so an insurer cannot rely on a detector violation, by you or by the tenant, to refuse a claim. The detector duties and their fines still apply (see "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors"), and the shield does not cover other negligence. (3) Double letting: no statute addresses renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period. You must deliver the unit fit and habitable at the start of the tenancy, and the one special rule is that a tenant who abandoned owing rent cannot displace a new tenant you leased to under the statutory reletting notice before the old tenant asked in writing to come back (see "Renting the Same Unit Twice"). (4) Payment-method fees: no statute bars or caps a fee a private landlord charges for paying rent by card or electronically; the convenience-fee rules that exist cover courts, public service districts and state agencies. Under this library's reading a fee for a payment method the tenant chooses is the price of an option, so state it in the lease, keep it to your actual cost and offer a fee-free way to pay (see "How Rent May Be Paid"). Other absences are explained in their own rows: no tenant possession bond ("No Possession Bond for Tenants"), no eviction defense for a late benefit or voucher payment ("Late Benefit Checks and Eviction"), no state rule on a tenant's bankruptcy ("When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy") and no truth-in-renting act ("No Truth-in-Renting Law").

title: Squatters and Other Questions Outside the Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText: These answers to questions landlords ask hold across West Virginia's whole Code and its agency and court rules, not only the landlord-tenant law. (1) Squatters: since July 10, 2025, an owner or authorized agent may ask a law enforcement officer to remove a squatter from a residential dwelling by a verified complaint, without an eviction, if the conditions in the statute are met; it does not reach a tenant, a former tenant or family members (see "Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants"). (2) Receipts: no statute requires a receipt for rent, even cash rent; the one duty is that if a tenant claiming the senior citizens' homestead tax relief asks, you must sign a statement of the year's gross rent, and willfully failing to is a misdemeanor (see "No Rent Receipt Requirement"). Give a written receipt for cash anyway. (3) Registration: there is no statewide landlord registration or rental license, and nothing makes registration a condition of filing or winning an eviction; cities may require registration of uninhabitable or vacant buildings (see "Landlord Registration"). (4) Business filings can stop a suit. An out-of-state LLC that owns income-producing real property here is transacting business and may not maintain an action until it gets a certificate of authority; an out-of-state corporation transacting business without one may not maintain a proceeding in circuit court; and an out-of-state limited partnership may not maintain a suit in any court until it registers. Each can still defend a suit, and its leases stay valid (see "Out-of-State Landlords"). (5) Assumed names: anyone renting under a name other than their own, or an entity's registered name, must first file the name with the Secretary of State. Willfully failing to is a misdemeanor (a fine of $25 to $100, up to 30 days in jail, or both), but no statute bars a suit for that reason. (6) Out-of-state parties: a nonresident who has an interest in, uses or possesses real property here, including a tenant who moved out of state afterward, is treated as appointing the Secretary of State to receive process in a circuit court case arising from it. The Secretary of State mails the papers by registered or certified mail, and a default judgment may follow if the person does not appear and defend within 30 days. The same rule reaches an out-of-state landlord. (7) Reporting duties that bind any person, such as reporting apparent child sexual abuse images seen in the course of business, are in "Police Requests and Reporting Duties".

title: Who May Appear in Court for an LLC or Corporation Landlord
bodyText: Who may appear for a landlord that is an LLC, corporation or partnership depends on the court. In magistrate court, a statute lets any party to a civil case appear and conduct it in person, by an agent or by a lawyer, and says an agent's appearance is not the unlawful practice of law; a magistrate or magistrate court employee may not act as anyone's agent. A summary eviction petition is verified by the owner or the owner's agent, and the court's petition form has a box for each. A court rule for magistrate courts adds that a corporation may appear by a West Virginia lawyer or by any of its officers or employees, and that a non-lawyer employed only to represent the corporation in legal matters must be a full-time employee. That rule names corporations only, and no statute or court rule says who may appear for an LLC or a partnership by name; how the rule fits with the statute's broader agent wording is a question of case law. The cautious course in magistrate court is to send an owner, member, manager, officer or regular employee who knows the facts, with written authority from the entity, or a lawyer, and not to hire an outside non-lawyer just to appear. In circuit court the court rules require every party, except one appearing for itself, to be represented by a lawyer admitted in West Virginia, and a statute makes it a crime for anyone without a license to appear as a lawyer for another in a court. Whether an entity can appear for itself through an officer or member there is also case law not searched, so use a lawyer for any circuit court step: a summary eviction filed in circuit court, an appeal from magistrate court, or a possession case of $2,500 or more that any party moves to circuit court. A property manager may act as your agent in magistrate court under the statute, but not as your lawyer in circuit court. An out-of-state LLC or corporation may also need a certificate of authority before it can bring the case; see "Out-of-State Landlords".

title: Police Requests and Reporting Duties
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you, as a landlord, to cooperate with the police in general, to answer officers' questions about a tenant, or to give officers a key or let them into a unit, apart from the court orders described below. The state Constitution protects people against unreasonable searches of their houses, and whether your consent lets officers into a tenant's unit is a question of case law; the cautious course is to ask for a warrant or the tenant's consent before opening a unit for police. One court-ordered duty names landlords. When a court authorizes a pen register or trap-and-trace device, or a wiretap, it may direct a landlord to give officers the information, facilities and technical help needed; you are paid reasonably for the help and reimbursed your expenses, and an order of this kind directs you not to reveal the device or the investigation to anyone unless the court allows. A wiretap assistance order cannot make you grant entry onto your premises or do anything beyond giving information, facilities or technical help. Reporting duties: landlords are not on the lists of people who must report suspected abuse or neglect of a child, or abuse, neglect or financial exploitation of a vulnerable adult, unless you also work in a listed role, such as a child care worker or an employee of a nursing home or other residential facility; anyone may still report. One duty binds anyone acting in the course of a business: since July 9, 2025, a person who, in the course and scope of employment or business, views an image on a computer or electronic device that is or appears to show a minor in sexually explicit conduct must report it immediately to local or state law enforcement or to the CyberTipline of the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. If someone at the property dies by violence or apparent suicide, suddenly while in apparent good health, or without a physician in attendance, the medical examiner must be notified immediately, and the statute names any person present or having knowledge among those who give the notice; calling 911 or the police meets it in practice. Related rows: police removal of squatters ("Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants"), drug-lab notices and nuisance closures ("Former Drug Laboratories", "Nuisance Laws and Rental Property"), crime-free addenda ("Drug-Free or Crime-Free Addenda"), tenants' calls for help ("Calls for Police or Emergency Help") and the optional "Criminal Activity" clause. Ask the city.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: West Virginia does not require a residential lease to be registered, filed or recorded, and recording does not change the tenant's rights or your duties under the landlord-tenant or deposit laws; nothing turns on whether the tenant is your relative. Recording matters for a long lease. A lease for more than five years must be made by deed, and it, or a memorandum of it, is valid against your creditors and later buyers from the time it is recorded in the county where the property is; until then it is void as to creditors and as to later buyers who pay value without notice of it. Instead of the whole lease you may record a memorandum signed by everyone who is a party to the lease and acknowledged as a deed would be, giving the names and addresses of landlord and tenant, a reference to the lease and its date, the description of the premises, the start and end dates of the term, and any extension or renewal rights and when they can be used; it gives notice only of what it says. To be recorded a document must be acknowledged before an officer such as a notary, and the county clerk may refuse, or record at one and a half times the usual fee, anything printed on both sides of the paper or in type smaller than 10-point. A lease is not a deed for the state's real estate transfer tax. Recording can also protect a tenant if the property is lost to foreclosure: a buyer at a trustee's sale may end an unexpired written lease that was never recorded, or was recorded after the deed of trust, on the notice the statute sets (90 days, or 30 days before the lease ends if sooner), but not a lease recorded first. For an ordinary lease of a year or two none of this is needed.

title: Lease Length, Formalities and Spouses
bodyText:
West Virginia sets no maximum term for a private residential lease; the term limits in the Code bind public bodies leasing their own property. The length of the lease changes the formalities. A lease for more than one year cannot be enforced unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the person it is enforced against or that person's agent (see "Written Leases and Long Terms"). A lease for more than five years must be made by deed, though no seal is needed, and it binds your creditors and later buyers only from the time it, or a memorandum of it, is recorded (see "Recording a Lease").

No statute requires your spouse to sign or consent to a lease, and that is so even if the property is your homestead. Dower and curtesy are abolished, West Virginia is not a community-property state, and a married owner may deal with property before a divorce court orders otherwise or a notice of the divorce case is recorded. One rule does reach married owners: a married person who conveys an interest in real estate must notify the other spouse before the conveyance or within 30 days after it, if dower would have attached to the property under the old law.

Whether a lease is a conveyance for this rule is not settled, so the cautious course for an individual owner who is married is to tell the spouse in writing or have the spouse sign the lease's optional acknowledgment ("Landlord's Spouse Acknowledgment" clause). Failing to notify does not affect the lease or the tenant: the statute creates no lien or claim against the interest conveyed, and its only effect is that in a divorce within five years the value of what was conveyed counts as marital property.

The homestead exemption protects an owner's principal home from creditors up to $5,000 and cannot be waived except with a consensual security interest; it adds no signing rule for a lease. If title is in more than one name, every owner should sign.

title: Type Size in Your Lease
bodyText: West Virginia sets no minimum point size for a residential lease, and no rule makes a lease, or a clause in it, unenforceable or inadmissible in court because of small print. The rule that does apply is the plain-language law: a written agreement for renting space to live in must use type of an easily readable size and ink that contrasts with the paper, as well as clear everyday words and captioned sections. A violation does not make the lease void, but if the tenant asks for a conforming lease and you refuse, the tenant can sue to have it rewritten, and the tenant cannot waive that right (see "Plain Language Leases"). Other West Virginia type-size rules, such as those for insurance policies, consumer credit cosigner notices, used-car disclaimers and self-storage default notices, do not reach a lease of a home. One rule matters if you record a long lease or a memorandum of lease: the county clerk may refuse to record an instrument printed on both sides of the paper or in type smaller than 10-point with at least two points between lines, or may record it at one and a half times the usual fee; a refusal does not affect the lease between you and the tenant (see "Recording a Lease"). Use at least 10-point type for anything you may record, and readable type throughout.

title: How Long You Have to Sue a Tenant
bodyText: West Virginia's landlord-tenant statutes set no deadline of their own for suing a tenant or former tenant; the general time limits apply, each counted from when the right to sue arises. A suit for money on a written lease signed by the tenant (or the tenant's agent) must generally be brought within ten years; on an oral lease, or a written one the tenant did not sign, within five years. Treat each missed rent payment as starting its own clock. If you sue for physical damage to the property as damage rather than as a breach of the lease, the cautious course is to sue within two years, because a personal action for damage to property has a two-year limit and which period a court applies is a question of case law. An unlawful detainer case for possession must be brought within three years after the unlawful detainer, and distress for rent within one year after the rent fell due. A judgment can be enforced by execution for ten years, and new executions can be issued within ten years after an unsatisfied one is returned. Only a written promise to pay, or a written acknowledgment from which a promise can be implied, signed by the tenant or the tenant's agent, starts a new period for the amount promised; no other promise does, and no statute says a partial payment does, so do not count on a payment to restart the clock; get a signed acknowledgment of the balance. A promise by one co-tenant does not extend the time against another co-tenant. Time does not run while a tenant who lived in West Virginia obstructs the suit by leaving the state, absconding or hiding; a bankruptcy stay pauses the clock for the stay and then for the rest of the period or one year, whichever is longer; and if a timely case is dismissed for a reason other than the merits, you may refile within one year. No West Virginia statute addresses a lease term that shortens the time to sue; this library's lease contains none.

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals
bodyText: West Virginia has no special rules for seasonal or vacation tenancies, and its landlord-tenant and security deposit statutes have no exclusion for short or transient stays. Whether a short-stay guest in a cabin, vacation home or room is a tenant, rather than a lodger, is a question of case law; the cautious course is to treat anyone who rents a dwelling from you under a rental agreement as a tenant, so the deposit rules, the habitability duties and the court eviction process apply. A seasonal lease for a fixed term ends on its last day without notice from either side, because no notice is needed for a tenancy whose term is to end at a set time; if the tenant stays on without your consent, see "Tenants Who Stay After the Lease Ends". On a property covered by the federal CARES Act, give at least 30 days' written notice to vacate before you require the tenant to leave (see "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties"). Your duty to supply reasonable heat, for a unit on a direct public utility connection, runs from October 1 to the last day of April. Taxes: a county or city may impose a hotel occupancy tax of 3 percent, which may be raised to as much as 6 percent, on sleeping accommodations the public may rent, including cabins, condominiums, lodges and tourist homes. It does not reach a boarding house, condominium, cabin, tourist home, apartment or home rented month to month or for 30 days or longer from the start, or a private home offering fewer than three rooms for no more than 10 days a year. Check with the county or city where the property is. Local rules: cities may not prohibit or effectively limit renting a property or regulate how long, how often or where it is rented, and may regulate activities arising from rental use only if the rule applies to all properties alike; how far that reaches is unsettled.

title: Special Districts and Your Lease
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule requires a lease to state, or you to tell a tenant, that the property lies in a special district, such as a business improvement district, community enhancement district, public service district, economic opportunity development district or tax increment development district, and none gives a tenant a vote or a board seat because the tenant rents there. District charges fall on owners.

A city's business improvement district levies service fees on commercial property, which the statute defines as real property in tax Class IV; Class IV is non-owner-occupied property inside a city, so a rental building there can be charged, and the fee is a lien on the property. A community enhancement district's assessments are a lien on the property and are paid by the owners; when you sell, you must disclose the assessment to the buyer in the contract, but nothing requires telling a tenant.

Representation follows ownership or residence: a business improvement district board must have a majority of commercial property owners; at least three members of a community enhancement board must live in the district, so a resident tenant could qualify; and at the hearing on creating a business improvement or county development district, any owner in the district and any resident of the city or county may be heard.

If you want a tenant to share a district charge, the lease must say so. A tenant's general promise to pay the taxes covers taxes, levies and assessments on the property, but not an assessment for a permanent local improvement, such as paving a street or sidewalk, unless the lease expressly says so. The optional clause "Special District Fees and Assessments" does that; for property-tax increases see "Passing On Property Tax and Insurance Increases", and for public service district water and sewer bills see "Tenant Utility Bills and Liens on Your Property".

Local ordinances creating a district set its own rules; read the ordinance.

title: Leasing When You Hold Only a Life Estate
bodyText: West Virginia law has no usufruct, the civil-law right to use another's property and keep its income. The closest West Virginia interest is a life estate, for example a parent who deeded a house to the children but kept the right to live in it or rent it out for life, or another interest that ends on an uncertain event. If you lease property in which you hold only a life estate or another uncertain interest, or a fee that ends if some contingency happens, and your interest ends during the tenancy, the tenant may stay until the end of the current year of the tenancy, paying rent. Rent payable in money is split between you or your estate and the people who take the property next. Whether those people are bound by the rest of a longer lease is a question of case law, so if you want a lease to run past your own interest, have the people who will take the property next sign it too. Where some of them cannot consent, for example because they are minors or not yet born, a person with an interest in the property may ask the circuit court to approve a lease of it; the court can do so if the lease promotes that person's interest without materially harming anyone else's, and with the consent of everyone then living who has a vested interest (a guardian may consent for a minor), or subject to the interest of anyone who refuses. Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends must return any security deposit owed, however that person got the interest. Tell a prospective tenant that you hold a life estate, and keep the names of the people who take next in your records, so the tenant knows who will be the landlord if your interest ends.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
West Virginia has no rule that every landlord-tenant notice must be written; each statute says for itself. These must be in writing. To end a year-to-year tenancy, either side gives written notice at least three months before the end of a year; for a shorter periodic tenancy the statute calls for like notice, or notice for one full period, so give it in writing too (see "Notice to End a Tenancy"). A lease may fix another notice period or provide that no notice is needed, and no notice is needed when a lease ends on a set date, but nothing lets a lease replace a written notice with a spoken one.

On a property covered by the federal CARES Act, federal law bars requiring the tenant to vacate until 30 days after you give a notice to vacate, whatever the lease says; it does not say the notice must be written, but give it in writing (see "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties"). If a tenant who owes rent abandons the unit, you post a written notice on the property requiring payment within one month, and to dispose of belongings you post and mail a written notice giving at least 30 days (60 if the tenant told you of active military duty). A tenant who abandoned and wants the unit back must tell you so in writing.

An heir or personal representative ending a lease after a tenant dies does so by a notice hand-delivered or mailed, which takes effect at the end of the second full month. After the tenancy ends you send the deposit with a written itemization, and if damage exceeds the deposit and needs a contractor you send written notice of that within the same period to get 15 more days. A pet or application fee is nonrefundable only if you both agree in writing. A tenant may ask in writing to see your record of deposit deductions, and you then have 72 hours.

After an eviction order you may dispose of belongings at once if the tenant tells you in writing they are abandoned. If you buy a rental at a trustee's sale, a tenant with an unexpired written lease gets 90 days' written notice or written notice at least 30 days before the lease ends, whichever is shorter, and a month-to-month tenant gets 30 days' written notice. A lease that bars assigning or subletting without leave means without your written consent.

If you and the tenant agreed to deal electronically, an email the tenant can print or store can satisfy some of these, but not a notice of default, eviction or the right to cure for the tenant's home (see "Electronic Leases and Records"). The cautious course is to put every notice in writing, deliver it by the method the statute names, and keep a copy.

title: Reselling Electricity or Gas to Tenants
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule sets a disclosure or lease statement for electricity or gas you submeter, allocate or bill to tenants, and none says outright whether doing so makes you a regulated utility. The Public Service Commission's electric rules point against it. An electric utility may not furnish electricity to any customer for resale unless the customer is in the business of distributing electricity as a public utility. Apartment houses, row houses, condominiums and other multi-unit residential dwellings should be individually metered rather than master metered unless the utility, the owner or another interested party shows by clear and convincing evidence that an exemption is proper. And if the owner of a multiple apartment building furnishes electricity to tenants as part of their monthly rent, the utility classes that service as commercial. The public utility law covers anyone engaged in a business that is, or is later held to be, a public service, and treats a buyer for resale as the utility's customer; whether a landlord who meters and charges tenants for electricity is a public utility depends on Commission decisions. The cautious course is to have each unit metered by the utility with the tenant as its customer, or to include electricity in the rent, and not to submeter and rebill electricity without the Commission's or a lawyer's confirmation. The gas rules have no resale bar or individual-metering rule; if a gas master meter is in your name, you are the customer, and federal pipeline-safety rules define a master meter system to include an apartment complex or housing project where the owner buys metered gas and resells it to tenants through its own piping, whether through a meter or through the rent; if you distribute gas that way, ask the Public Service Commission whether its pipeline-safety rules apply to your piping.

title: Tenant Energy-Use Data for Benchmarking
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule lets a lease clause authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy or water usage data to you, requires a utility to give an owner its tenants' usage data, or requires you to benchmark a residential building's energy use. The only benchmarking provision is in the State Building Code, which treats building energy benchmarking in commercial structures as an allowable option for improved energy efficiency, not a duty. A tenant who holds the account can share the tenant's own bills or usage history with you, and a utility may have its own release form, so if you want the data, ask the tenant to share it or to sign the utility's form. The library does not offer a lease clause for this, because no statute makes such a clause binding on the utility and the usage data belongs to the tenant's account; you may add your own consent clause with legal advice.

title: Renting a Furnished Home
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule sets special terms for a furnished rental: there is no separate or higher furniture deposit, no required inventory and no set return standard for furnishings. Because West Virginia does not cap security deposits, nothing turns on whether the unit is furnished when you set the deposit. At the end of the tenancy you may apply the deposit to damages you suffer because the tenant did not comply with the lease, less reasonable wear and tear, and to other damages or charges the lease provides for, listed on the written itemization.

A signed inventory with each item's condition at move-in is the best evidence for any deduction; the library's optional Furnishings clause provides one and makes the tenant answerable for damage the tenant's household or guests cause through fault or lack of reasonable care. Any appliance you supply with the unit must be kept in good and safe working order. If you go to court for possession, the judge sets the move-out time considering, among other things, whether the property is furnished or unfurnished.

title: Energy-Efficiency Charges on a Utility Meter
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule ties an energy-efficiency or conservation charge to a utility meter or to the premises so that it passes to the next customer or occupant, or requires you to tell a new tenant about such a charge or take it off the rent. Where the Public Service Commission's residential conservation service rules apply, an electric or gas utility recovers what it spends on labor and materials to buy or install a residential energy conservation measure from the residential customer for whom the work was done, and may charge that customer for a detailed (Class A) energy audit no more than $15 per dwelling unit or the actual cost, whichever is less. Nothing in those rules moves the charge to a later customer at the same address, so if you are the customer who signs up, the charge stays with you. No statute or rule sets what a landlord may charge for submetered water; before billing tenants for water at all, read the library's note on submetering, because the Commission's water rule bars a customer from reselling water unless it is a public utility.

title: Window and Portable Air Conditioners
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule gives a residential tenant a right to install a window or portable air conditioner, limits a lease term that restricts them, or requires the lease to disclose such a restriction, and none requires you to provide air conditioning. So a lease may allow, condition or forbid window units, for example by requiring your written consent, a secure installation that does not damage the window frame, and removal at move-out. If you do supply air conditioning, whether central or a window unit, it is one of the facilities and appliances you supplied, and you must keep it in good and safe working order. Your heat and hot-water duties are separate and do not cover cooling. The State Building Code adopts the International Property Maintenance Code, which a local jurisdiction may reject; check any local property maintenance code for cooling or window rules.

title: Smart Locks and App-Based Entry
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule regulates smart locks, keypad or keyless entry, or app-based access systems in residential rentals: none requires you to offer a physical key, limits what entry data you may collect or keep, or sets rules for issuing and ending app logins. No West Virginia law lets a domestic-violence survivor require whoever manages a connected device's accounts, including a landlord who issues smart-lock or thermostat logins, to cut off another person's access. Because West Virginia also has no statute on when a landlord may enter, the lease sets the rules: if you use a smart lock, say who will hold codes or logins, how and when you will change them (at least between tenants and when a tenant reports a lost key or a compromised code), and how you will enter. The library's existing rows on entry, keys, security devices and lock changes after a protective order apply to a smart lock as to any other lock.

title: Utility Charges and the Security Deposit
bodyText: West Virginia's deposit law names utilities among the things a security deposit may cover. When the tenancy ends you may apply the deposit to unpaid utilities that were billed to and paid by you, that the lease makes the tenant's obligation, and that the tenant has not paid; bills you have not paid yourself, or charges the lease does not put on the tenant, do not qualify. The same law defines rent as all money owed or paid to you under the rental agreement other than a security deposit, a nonrefundable fee or money paid for damage the tenant caused, so within the deposit law a utility charge that the lease makes the tenant owe you is part of the rent; whether that reading carries over to eviction or late fees outside the deposit law is unsettled. List each deduction on the written itemization you deliver with the balance of the deposit within the notice period. Deposits the tenant paid to a utility are a separate matter: they belong to the tenant as the utility's customer and are returned by the utility, not by you. Under the Public Service Commission's rules an electric, gas, water or sewer utility refunds a residential deposit with interest after twelve consecutive months of bills paid on time, or credits it to the final bill, and a public service district or municipal water or sewer system holds a tenant's deposit until the tenant discontinues service and then refunds it with interest. Do not hold or apply a utility's deposit, and do not ask the tenant to pay you a second deposit for utilities the tenant pays the provider directly.

title: Past Utility Bills and Energy Costs
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to give a prospective or current tenant past utility bills, energy-use data or an estimate of utility costs, or to attach a utility disclosure to the lease, even where the tenant will pay for heat or cooling. The Public Service Commission's rules on explaining rates, meter readings and bills run from the utility to its own customer, so a tenant who opens an account in the tenant's own name can get that information from the utility. If the tenant will pay any utilities, the lease should say which ones, and whether the tenant pays the provider directly or reimburses you; the library's utility clauses do that. Sharing a typical monthly cost when an applicant asks is good practice but optional; if you do, give accurate figures.

title: Getting Copies of a Tenant's Utility Shutoff Notices
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or Public Service Commission rule lets you, as the owner, sign up on your own, or by a separate authorization, to be told when a tenant's utility service is about to be shut off. The Commission's electric and gas rules put the choice with the account holder instead: if a residential customer, or the customer's agent, asks the utility to contact a relative or responsible third party before any termination or other material action on the account, the utility must send every written termination notice to both the customer and that person, and must give the required personal-contact notice (a visit, call or message) to that person, after which it need not make personal contact with the customer.

A tenant who holds the electric or gas account can name you, and the library's optional clause asks the tenant to do so. The rules do not define a responsible third party, so ask each utility whether it will accept a landlord. The water and sewer rules have no such designation. A person who guarantees a customer's account in place of a cash deposit receives copies of electric and gas disconnection notices, and may ask for copies of water and sewer notices from a utility other than a public service district, but a guarantor is liable for the guaranteed amount.

When the account is yours, as landlord of a master-metered building or as a customer who does not live at a single-unit rental, the utility must post a termination notice at the property at least five days before the shutoff (for water and sewer, five days not counting weekends and holidays), so your tenants will learn of a missed bill. These rules bind utilities the Commission regulates; ask any other utility what it offers.

title: No Right to Cut Off Utilities You Bill
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or Public Service Commission rule lets you interrupt or shut off a utility that you submeter, allocate or bill to a tenant when the tenant does not pay, or sets a procedure for doing so. The deposit law lets a landlord use submetering equipment, energy allocation equipment or a ratio utility billing system if the rental agreement so provides, but it says nothing about cutting service off. The Commission's disconnection rules (written notice, personal contact, no shutoffs on certain days or in freezing weather) bind public utilities, not landlords. Two of its rules also caution against rebilling at all: an electric utility may not furnish electricity to a customer for resale unless the customer is in the business of distributing electricity as a public utility, and a water utility's customer may not resell water unless it is in that business. Do not cut off a utility to collect a bill or to force a tenant out. For a unit supplied by direct public utility connections you must supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April, unless the tenant controls the installation. Collect unpaid utility charges that the lease makes the tenant's obligation through the courts, or at the end of the tenancy from the security deposit for utilities you were billed for and paid.

title: Billing Tenants by Submeter or Formula: What to Check First
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule sets a disclosure form, type-size rule, unit threshold, billing limit or late-fee cap for utilities you submeter, allocate or bill back to tenants. The deposit law allows submetering equipment, energy allocation equipment or a ratio utility billing system if the rental agreement so provides, so the lease must say which utilities you bill and how each charge is figured; the library's Utility Billing clause does that.

Before billing water, check the Public Service Commission's water rule: a utility customer may not resell water furnished by a public utility unless the customer is in the business of distributing water as a public utility. An owner who furnishes water to tenants as part of their monthly rent is served by the water utility as a commercial customer, so including water in the rent is the arrangement the rules recognize. The Public Service Commission's water rules do not say whether measuring each tenant's water with a submeter, or splitting the bill by a formula, and charging the tenant counts as resale.

The cautious course is to include water in the rent or have each tenant take service in the tenant's own name, unless the Commission or your lawyer confirms that separate billing is allowed. Electricity raises the same question; see the library's note on reselling electricity. The sewer rule bases sewer charges on the water meter and has no resale bar.

title: Moving Utilities Into the Tenant's Name
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule sets a deadline for a tenant to move utilities into the tenant's own name, or lets you cut off service left in your name when the tenant does not; no protective-order statute directs a utility to move a household account to a protected person, and no statute lets a deploying servicemember suspend utilities. What the Public Service Commission's rules do say: while an account is yours, you stay responsible for service until the utility receives your notice to stop it (at least three days' notice for electric and gas unless your contract sets another period; for water and sewer, notice during business hours, with service stopped by the end of the next business day).

A change in the customer at a water or sewer address requires a new application, and an applicant must say whether the applicant is a tenant or an owner and, if a tenant, give the owner's name and address. A utility may not refuse a new tenant service because a previous occupant left a bill unpaid, unless they were members of the same household when the bill was run up. A divorce court may order a spouse to move utility accounts into the other spouse's name, so the account holder can change during a lease.

Don't cut off service to make a tenant act: you must keep running water, hot water and, from October 1 through April, heat supplied to a unit on direct public utility connections unless the tenant controls the installation. Set a transfer date in the lease instead; the library's optional clause does that.

title: Detector Tampering Charges
bodyText:
West Virginia has no law that sets or authorizes a fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide detector, so do not put a flat tampering fee in the lease. Under this library's reading of the state debt collection law, a charge added because a tenant broke the lease needs a statute behind it, and none exists for this; if that law reaches rent, collecting such a fee could cost you the tenant's actual damages plus a penalty of up to $1,000 per violation (see the consumer protection rows).

What you can do is have the lease make the tenant reimburse the reasonable actual cost of repairing or replacing a detector that the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or a guest removed, disconnected or disabled, or damaged through a lack of reasonable care (see the optional detector tampering cost clause). Keep the receipt. Tampering is also an offense. In buildings the State Fire Code covers, which is every building except one used wholly as a dwelling for no more than two families, no one may make a fire extinguishing system or fire warning system inoperative or inaccessible except as needed for emergencies, maintenance, drills or testing.

Fire officials may issue citations for tampering with, or disabling, fire detection equipment and fire alarm systems, and violating a State Fire Code safety rule is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $100 to $1,000, up to 90 days in jail, or both. In a one- or two-family dwelling you do not live in, the tenant must do routine maintenance on the smoke detectors, and a violation of the detector statute is a misdemeanor (see the detector rows).

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: West Virginia has no law requiring you to have balconies, decks, porches, stairs or other raised exterior structures of a rental inspected on a schedule, by an engineer or otherwise, or to report on them. Your general duties cover them instead. You must deliver the rental fit and habitable and keep it that way, make the repairs needed to keep it so (unless the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest made them necessary through lack of reasonable care), keep it up to applicable health, safety, fire and housing codes, and, in a building with more than one unit, keep the common areas under your control clean, safe and in repair. A rotted deck or loose railing can breach those duties, so look at them yourself, especially before each new tenancy and after storms, and fix what you find. New construction and renovation must meet the State Building Code in counties and cities that have adopted it, and a county or city may adopt a property maintenance code with its own upkeep standards; check locally.

title: Certificates of Occupancy
bodyText: West Virginia does not require you to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy, to give the tenant a copy, or to put a statement about one in the lease, and no statute bars collecting rent for a unit without one. There is also no statewide rental license or rental certificate. Getting a certificate is required in some cases. Under the State Fire Code, the owner or occupant of a new building, or of an existing building in which half or more of the space has been renovated or reconstructed, must obtain a certificate of occupancy, including from the State Fire Marshal's Office, before the building is occupied or used for its intended purpose. That rule covers apartment buildings and other buildings except those used wholly as dwellings for no more than two families. A county or city that has adopted the State Building Code may also issue occupancy permits under its own program. Whether a lease or rent is enforceable for a unit occupied without a required certificate is not settled by statute, so do not let a tenant move into a new or heavily renovated building until the certificate issues; the State Fire Marshal can also order a hazardous building closed to occupants.

title: Common-Area Lighting
bodyText: West Virginia sets no lighting standard for the halls, stairways, entrances or other common areas of a rental building, and has no rule letting a lease make a tenant pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own electric service. Your general duties still apply. In a building with more than one dwelling unit you must keep the common areas under your control that are kept for your tenants clean, safe and in repair; you must keep the electrical facilities you supply in good and safe working order; and you must keep the property up to applicable health, safety, fire and housing codes. A dark stairway or entry can breach those duties. Lighting levels may come from a property maintenance code your county or city has adopted, or from the national Life Safety Code that the State Fire Code adopts; check with your local code official. The State Fire Code's own text calls for emergency and exit lighting only in new buildings more than 75 feet high. On billing: the Public Service Commission's electric rules define residential service as a tenant's own household use, extended only to yard, garage or barn lighting used by that resident alone, so lights that also serve other tenants fall outside it. For that reason this library does not offer a clause making a tenant pay for common-area lights; keep shared lights on your own account, or get advice before writing your own clause.

title: Which Fire and Building Code Editions Apply
bodyText: West Virginia's statutes do not name the edition of any fire, building or housing code that applies to a rental. They leave that to the State Fire Commission's rules, and those rules adopt fixed editions, so a newer national edition does not apply until the Commission adopts it by a new rule. The State Fire Code (effective July 1, 2026) adopts the 2021 editions of NFPA 1, the Fire Code, and NFPA 101, the Life Safety Code, with West Virginia additions, and applies statewide as a minimum. By its own terms it does not apply to buildings used wholly as dwellings for no more than two families, though the statute on smoke and carbon monoxide detectors still applies to those homes (see the detector rows). The State Building Code (effective August 1, 2022, and set to expire August 1, 2027 unless replaced) adopts the 2018 International Building, Residential, Existing Building, Plumbing, Mechanical, Fuel Gas, Property Maintenance and Swimming Pool and Spa Codes, the 2015 International Energy Conservation Code for residential buildings, the 2017 ICC/ANSI A117.1 accessibility standard and the 2020 National Electrical Code, each with West Virginia changes. It has force only in a county or city that has adopted it, it applies only going forward (to building and renovation work, not as a retrofit duty for existing buildings), and a county or city may reject the Property Maintenance Code. In two places the Building Code names different editions (the 2018 and 2021 Life Safety Code, and the 2015 Residential Code for sprinkler floor protection), so ask the local code official which one governs your work. The smoke detector statute points to the current edition of the State Fire Code, and the fair housing accessibility safe harbor names ANSI A117.1 without an edition.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: West Virginia does not require you, at any size of complex, to adopt a key-control policy, keep a log of keys issued and returned, restrict who holds master keys, or run background checks on employees or contractors who can get into units. It also has no biometric privacy law covering a fingerprint, face or other biometric door-entry system. No statute sets when you may enter a unit either, so your entry rights come from the lease (see the entry and keys rows). Key control is still sound practice, and whether an owner can be liable for harm caused by a staff member or former tenant who used a key is a question for case law. The cautious course: issue keys against a signed receipt, log who holds master keys and codes, keep them locked up, rekey or reset codes between tenants and when a key is lost or a staff member leaves, screen anyone you give key access, and enter only as the lease allows. If you use a biometric entry system, tell tenants what it collects and offer a key or code alternative.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: West Virginia does not require you to carry liability insurance on a rental, to show tenants proof of coverage or tell them whether you are insured, or to register a certificate of insurance with a city or county. Insurance is still prudent: you must keep the rental fit and habitable and, in a building with more than one unit, keep the common areas safe, and no West Virginia statute says whether a lease can excuse you from liability for injuries (see the liability waiver row). Your mortgage lender, a condominium or homeowners association, or a housing program may require coverage, and your lease may require the tenant to carry renter's insurance (see the renter's insurance rows). A state law in the municipal home rule section says a city may regulate activities that arise from renting only through rules that apply uniformly to all properties, rented or not, but how far that reaches is unsettled; check any local rental registration or licensing program for an insurance requirement.

title: Other Facilities With Their Own Rules
bodyText: Beyond the general repair duties (see the landlord repair duties row), some building facilities carry their own West Virginia rules. Elevators: if your building has a passenger elevator, you must register it with the Division of Labor; every elevator in use five years or more must be inspected each year; it may not run without a current certificate of operation, which expires a year after inspection and must be posted in the elevator; and you must make the repairs an inspection report lists before a certificate issues. These rules do not apply to an elevator inside a single-family home. Pools and spas: a pool, spa or hot tub at an apartment complex or condominium is a recreational water facility, and the owner or operator needs a construction permit to build or renovate it and an operating permit, displayed at the pool, to run it; a pool at a single home housing no more than three families, used only by residents and their non-paying guests, is outside the rule. Boilers: a steam boiler carrying more than 15 pounds of pressure per square inch needs an operating permit from the Commissioner of Labor, except boilers in private residences used solely as residences and sectional boilers; ask the Division of Labor whether a boiler serving an apartment building is covered. Heaters: the State Fire Code bans unvented fuel-fired heaters in every building it covers except one- and two-family dwellings, so do not supply or allow them in a building with three or more units. Fire protection systems must carry an inspection tag, and buildings other than one- and two-family dwellings need a sprinkler and window sign (see the sprinkler sign row). West Virginia has no rule on automatic garage door openers.

title: Sprinkler and Window Signs
bodyText: West Virginia does not require a lease to say whether the building has fire sprinklers, and has no grant, loan or tax credit for sprinkler retrofits. The State Fire Code (effective July 1, 2026) does require a posted sign. Every residential occupancy except a one- or two-family dwelling must prominently display a sign stating whether the building has an approved automatic sprinkler system and whether its windows can be opened or broken in an emergency. The rule does not say where the sign goes or what it must look like, so put it where tenants and visitors entering the building will see it, and keep it accurate. "Residential occupancy" is defined in the national Life Safety Code the rule adopts; if your building has three or more dwelling units, the cautious course is to post the sign. The same rule requires automatic sprinklers in all new buildings it covers, other than industrial buildings, and an inspection tag on each fire protection system showing who did the work, the date of the test and the results; maintenance, repair and inspection work done for pay must be done by a company with a certified employee. You may also state the building's sprinkler status in the lease; if you do, make it match the sign.

title: No Radiator Cover Requirement
bodyText: West Virginia has no law requiring you to put covers or guards on steam or hot-water radiators in a rental, to offer them on request, or to add a lease rider about them. The only radiator-shielding rules are for licensed child care centers and residential child care facilities. Your general duties still apply: you must keep the heating facilities you supply in good and safe working order, and where the unit is served by direct public utility connections you must supply reasonable heat from October 1 through the last day of April, unless the heat is generated by an installation in the tenant's exclusive control. If a tenant with young children or a disability asks for a radiator cover, consider providing one; a request tied to a disability may be a reasonable accommodation or modification request under fair housing law (see the fair housing rows).

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText:
West Virginia does not require you to supply a stove, range or refrigerator in a rental. What matters is what you supply or agree to supply: any appliance you provide, or promise in the lease or orally to provide, you must keep in good and safe working order. List the appliances you include in the lease (see the appliances-included clause), and if an appliance at the property belongs to the tenant or was left by a prior occupant, say in the lease that you do not supply or maintain it (see the appliances-excluded clause).

If a gas or other fuel-burning stove is in a newly built unit, a carbon monoxide detector is required there (see the detector rows). A unit with no refrigerator, stove or sink of its own, whose occupant shares one with other units, makes its occupant a "roomer"; the security deposit law still covers roomers as tenants.

title: Asbestos in Rental Buildings
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to inspect a rental for asbestos, disclose asbestos to tenants or prospective tenants, or tell tenants before asbestos work. West Virginia regulates asbestos work instead, and the Department of Health's asbestos rule applies to every building owner, with no exception for residential buildings. Before any renovation or demolition, you must have the building inspected for asbestos by a licensed asbestos inspector. Any asbestos abatement project, meaning the repair, removal, enclosure or encapsulation of material containing more than 1% asbestos (other than removing less than 3 square or linear feet during ordinary maintenance), must be designed, supervised and carried out by state-licensed people, and you must notify the Department at least 10 working days before it starts, with the fee. In an emergency the notice may follow the event; projects under 160 square feet or 260 linear feet of material, outside schools, may be reported in a weekly summary instead. You may delegate these duties in writing to the person who runs the building, and the notice duty to the contractor. The contractor must make sure the work area meets clearance standards before anyone moves back in. Removing asbestos floor tile or sheet vinyl in a single-family home is done by licensed resilient floor covering workers and needs no notice. Violations can bring civil penalties of $250 to $5,000 each and are misdemeanors. The state air rule also adopts the federal asbestos emission standards, which can add duties before demolition or renovation; they are not covered here. The notices go to the state, not to tenants; if work will disturb asbestos in or near an occupied unit, telling the tenants beforehand is sensible.

title: Bed Bugs and Pest Treatment
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule requires a residential tenant to report bed bugs or other pests, to let you in for inspection or treatment, or to prepare the unit, and none says who pays for pest treatment in a rental. The state's only bed bug statute applies to hotels with ten or more bed chambers (see the bed bugs row). Your general duties still apply: you must keep the unit fit and habitable and make the repairs needed to keep it so, except repairs needed primarily because of a lack of reasonable care by the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent; the statute does not require repairs while the tenant is behind on rent, unless your lease promises more.

Because the law leaves cooperation to the lease, the library offers an optional clause: the tenant reports suspected infestations, allows entry under the lease's entry terms, follows written preparation instructions, and reimburses the actual cost of treatment and resulting repairs only when the infestation was caused primarily by that lack of reasonable care; otherwise treatment follows your repair duties under the lease and the law. Whether a particular infestation makes a unit unfit is for the courts. If you apply pesticides yourself, the state pesticide rules apply (see the pest control notice row).

title: Defective Drywall
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to tell tenants or prospective tenants about defective drywall, such as the corrosive imported drywall that some states regulate, and no West Virginia law sets drywall inspection or replacement duties for rentals. Your general duties still apply: you must deliver and keep the unit fit and habitable and in line with applicable health, safety, fire and housing codes, and keep its electrical, plumbing, heating and other facilities in good and safe working order, which corrosive drywall can damage. If you know a unit has defective drywall, telling prospective tenants before they sign is the cautious course, because saying nothing about a known defect can create liability under general law.

title: Contamination Disclosures
bodyText:
Three West Virginia rules can require you to tell tenants about contamination.

Hazardous waste: if the property or the ground beneath it was ever used to store, treat or dispose of hazardous waste, and you owned or had an interest in the property at that time or know of that use, you must say so in the lease itself (see the Hazardous Waste Disclosure clause). This applies to every lease, whatever its length, and a violation of the hazardous waste law can bring state civil penalties and injunctions.

Environmental covenants: if a state or federal cleanup left an environmental covenant (called a land use covenant in the state's voluntary remediation program) on the property, the covenant runs with the land, may restrict uses such as residential use, wells or digging, and can bind lessees. The person the Department of Environmental Protection requires, which in the voluntary program includes the property owner, must give a copy to each person in possession of the property.

Give each tenant a copy, attach it to the lease, and follow any notice the covenant itself requires, such as notice within 10 days after a transfer of a specified interest.

Former drug laboratories: you must disclose a clandestine drug laboratory identified on the property to any potential occupant (see the drug laboratory row).

No other West Virginia law requires you to tell tenants about other contamination, about a federal Superfund listing or about brownfield status, and none requires a residential tenant to notify you of a release.

title: Local Health Department Rules
bodyText: West Virginia has no health districts that issue rental regulations, and no statute or rule requires you to give a tenant a copy of health department rules on request or to refer a tenant to a health agency. Each county or city is served by a local board of health. It administers the state public health laws on general sanitation and on the sanitation of housing, investigates nuisances affecting public health, and may adopt its own local health rules. A new or amended local rule takes effect only if the county commission or other appointing authority approves it within 30 days (an emergency rule takes effect at once but lapses if not approved within 30 days), and approved rules are kept by the county or city clerk as public records. No state health rule sets standards for ordinary rental housing. The state general sanitation rule covers hotels, motels (including tourist cabins and cottages), bed and breakfast inns, labor camps, campgrounds, care facilities and similar places, which need a health department permit to operate; if you rent rooms or cabins to travelers, check that rule. For ordinary leases, your duty to keep the unit in line with applicable health, safety, fire and housing codes still applies (see the repair duties row), so ask your local health department whether it has adopted any rule on housing.

title: Open Code and Condemnation Orders
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to give tenants or prospective tenants copies of inspection reports, code-violation notices, repair or vacate orders, or condemnation or unfitness orders, or to disclose them before signing. One exception: if a clandestine drug laboratory was identified on the property, your disclosure to any potential occupant must include the related enforcement actions (see the drug laboratory row). Orders become known in other ways. A State Fire Marshal order to repair or demolish a hazardous building, or to remove dangerous materials, must be obeyed within 30 days unless appealed; it is recorded in the county's general lien book, which gives notice to anyone later dealing with the property, and if it has to be mailed to you it is also posted on the building's door or main entrance. If a city code enforcement agency gets an administrative search warrant to inspect a building, it must give the tenant a copy five days before entering, and a city's notice before it closes or demolishes an unsafe building is posted on the property. Counties may also order unsafe or unsanitary buildings repaired, vacated or demolished. Entering, without permission, a building posted as condemned by a city or county as unfit for human habitation is a crime. Your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable and in line with applicable codes continues (see the unfit or condemned units row), and telling a prospective tenant about any open order before signing is the cautious course.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate
bodyText: West Virginia has no lead-safe or lead-free certificate, registry, registration or periodic lead inspection for rental housing, and there is no lead certificate to attach to the lease. Federal law does not require one either: for housing built before 1978 you must disclose what you know about lead-based paint and hand over any reports you have, but you are not required to inspect for lead or reduce lead hazards (see the Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause). What West Virginia does regulate is lead work. Only state-licensed people may carry out a lead inspection, lead risk assessment or lead abatement, and before a lead abatement project (work meant to permanently eliminate lead-based paint hazards) the owner must notify the Department of Health 10 days ahead and pay its fee; the homeowner exemption does not cover a home occupied by tenants (see the lead abatement row). Ordinary renovation and repair work is not abatement under the state law, though federal renovation rules not covered here may apply. If a child living in the home has two consecutive blood lead tests at or above 8 micrograms per deciliter, the child is referred to the Department for an investigation of the home to find lead sources, and the state may order lead hazards reduced or abated when they may result in child lead poisoning. If you do have a licensed inspector or risk assessor check the property, keep the report, because you must give it to future tenants with the federal disclosure.

title: Lead Notices to Tenants
bodyText:
West Virginia has no lead notice, certificate, pamphlet or packet of its own that you must give tenants. The only lead disclosure for a rental is the federal one for housing built before 1978 (other than housing for the elderly or people with disabilities, and studio or other zero-bedroom units unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there). Before the tenant is bound by the lease, you must give the tenant an EPA-approved lead hazard pamphlet, such as Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home; disclose any lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards you know of, with what you know about them; and give the tenant any records or reports you have, including those on common areas.

The lease, or an attachment to it, must contain the federal Lead Warning Statement, your disclosure, a list of the records provided, the tenant's acknowledgment and the signatures and dates of you, the tenant and any agent (see the Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause). If a leasing agent acts for you, the agent must make sure these steps are done and the attachment must include the agent's statement. Keep the signed disclosure for at least 3 years from the start of the lease. If disclosure comes after the tenant has offered to rent, complete it before you accept the offer and let the tenant review it and change the offer.

A person who knowingly violates the federal disclosure law is liable to the tenant for three times the damages, plus court costs, attorney fees and expert witness fees, and faces federal penalties; it does not void the lease. West Virginia's own lead notices go to the state, not to tenants: before a lead abatement project, the owner notifies the Department of Health (see the lead abatement row).

Federal law also exempts a lease of housing a certified inspector has found free of lead-based paint, a lease of 100 days or less that cannot be renewed or extended, and a renewal where you already gave every required disclosure and have learned nothing new.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared Meters
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to tell a prospective tenant about a former military ordnance site nearby, about a permit you have applied for to demolish the unit, or that a gas or electric meter in the tenant's name also serves other units or common areas. Related rules: if you bill tenants through submetering, energy allocation or a ratio billing system, the rental agreement must provide for it, so a tenant-paid meter that also carries common-area or other-unit use should be addressed in the lease (see the utility apportionment row). Planned demolition does not end a lease by itself: a fixed-term lease runs to its end unless it says otherwise, and a periodic tenancy needs the notice the law or the lease requires. Before you renovate or demolish a building, you must have it inspected for asbestos by a licensed inspector and notify the Department of Health before any asbestos abatement (see the asbestos row). Telling a prospective tenant about a planned demolition before signing is the cautious course.

title: Pest Control and Pesticide Use
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to tell tenants about a pest control contract or to give notice before pesticides are applied in a rental, and none requires a pest control company to notify tenants. The pesticide law instead regulates who may apply pesticides. A business that applies pesticides for hire needs a state pesticide application business license, and the people applying must be certified applicators or registered technicians working under a certified applicator's supervision.

Under the Department of Agriculture's rule, a business that applies pesticides on its own property and not for hire, such as an apartment complex, is a regulated pesticide application business that must use certified applicators or trained registered technicians and license each location. A landlord doing general pest control on its own rental property of four rental units or less is exempt from that licensing if it uses only generally available, ready-to-use products such as prepared baits, aerosols or foggers, and only non-pressurized pump sprayers or dusters.

The statute separately frees unlicensed people using pest control products sold at ordinary retail stores from the for-hire license, but the rule's four-unit limit is narrower, so the cautious course with more than four units, or with any other product or equipment, is to hire a licensed pest control company. For termite treatment of a building with a domestic well, the company must get from you the location of every well within 100 feet and how it was built. The state also keeps a registry of people with a doctor-certified sensitivity to pesticide drift, which it shares with pesticide businesses for voluntary notification.

Entering a unit for treatment follows your lease's entry terms, and telling tenants beforehand which product will be used and how to prepare is sensible.

title: Private Wells Serving Rentals
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to test a private well that serves a rental or to give tenants or prospective tenants well water test results. Four related rules apply. First, a larger system is regulated: if your well or water system regularly supplies water for drinking through pipes to at least 15 service connections, or to an average of at least 25 people a day for at least 60 days a year (as a large apartment building, complex or park may), it is a public water system. It then needs a Department of Health permit to operate, must be run under the state rule and the federal drinking water regulations that rule adopts, including their testing and reporting, and must give public notice of any failure to comply; federal rules require that notice to go to the people the system serves, which includes your tenants; the federal monitoring details are not covered here. Second, drilling, altering or abandoning a well needs a permit that you and a certified well driller apply for together; when it issues the permit, the Department gives you information on why and how to sample the water, and it may inspect and sample a well, with the owner or occupant required to give access. Third, anyone with a right to possess the land, owner or tenant, must keep every water well, in use or abandoned, covered strongly enough that no one can fall in. Fourth, if an operator plans a horizontal gas well pad within 1,500 feet, it must offer the surface owner testing of a water well actually used for drinking and send the results to whoever asked. Testing a well that serves tenants and sharing the results is sensible, though not required.

title: Chemical Exposure Warnings
bodyText: West Virginia has no law like California's Proposition 65 requiring you to post signs or give tenants warnings about chemicals known to cause cancer, birth defects or other reproductive harm in a rental building, its parking areas or common areas. The state's health warning signs apply to other businesses, such as the birth-defect warning that alcohol retailers must post. The specific disclosures West Virginia does require for rentals are covered elsewhere: hazardous waste once stored, treated or disposed of on the property, environmental covenants and former drug laboratories (see the contamination disclosures row), and, under federal law, lead-based paint in housing built before 1978 (see the Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause).

title: Code Variances and Tenants
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to give tenants a copy of, or attach to the lease, a variance, exception or waiver from a health, sanitary, housing, building or fire code that applies to your property. West Virginia has no statewide sanitary or housing code for ordinary rental housing; county and city codes and local health department rules may have their own variance procedures, so follow any conditions a local variance sets. Some state health rules allow a variance granted to the owner. For example, the Department of Health may approve in writing, before the work is done, a variance for a private water well that cannot meet the rule's standards, such as its required distance from a septic tank, but only if the well will not be contaminated and the health of the people using its water will not be endangered; it then tests the water and may require a treatment unit. If a variance affects something your tenants use, such as the well that supplies their water, giving them a copy is sensible though not required. A variance changes only the rule it names; your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable still applies.

title: Association Documents and Your Tenant
bodyText:
When you rent out a unit in a condominium, cooperative or planned community, no West Virginia statute or rule requires you to give the tenant the association's declaration, bylaws or rules, to tell the tenant about the association's obligations, or to put an owner's or tenant's statement about the association documents in the lease. Two rules reach some leases. First, a lease of 20 years or more, counting renewal options, makes the tenant a purchaser under the Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act.

Before that lease is signed, you as unit owner must give the tenant a copy of the declaration (other than plats and plans), the bylaws, the association's rules and a resale certificate stating, among other things, the assessments and other fees, unpaid assessments, reserves, budget, pending suits, insurance and known violations. The association must give you the certificate within 10 days of your request and may charge a reasonable fee for it. Until the certificate is provided and for five days after, or until the conveyance, whichever comes first, the purchaser may cancel, and these rights cannot be waived by agreement.

Exemptions include a disposition the purchaser may cancel at any time without penalty and some small or low-assessment planned communities; older communities are covered too. That a long lease is a disposition under these rules is this library's reading of the definitions; follow the rule for any lease of 20 years or more. Second, if the unit is in an older condominium under the Unit Property Act, every written instrument dealing with a unit, including a lease, must state the name by which the property is identified and the unit's designation; the condominium unit clause does this.

Even where nothing is required, give the tenant the documents and have the tenant acknowledge them: the association's rules bind you as owner, and the lease is how they bind your tenant. If the declaration gives lessees the vote on some matters, those lessees also get notice of the meetings and access to records on those matters.

title: No Communal or Tribal Land Lease Approval
bodyText: West Virginia has no communal, tribal or native land system, and no statute or rule requires a government officer to approve a residential lease, or voids it, because of how the land is held.

title: Home Child Care in a Rental
bodyText:
No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to let a tenant run a child care business in a rental, or sets conditions such as parent waivers or insurance if you allow one, so the lease decides. State law regulates the care itself: a family child care home provides care for pay to four to six children under six at a time, counting the provider's own, in the provider's residence, and a family child care facility serves seven to twelve; both operate under the Department of Human Services' licensing or registration rules.

West Virginia also makes a home-based business run by the owner or tenant inside a dwelling a permitted use for local zoning purposes, but that rule expressly does not override an agreement restricting the use of land, so a lease that limits the property to residential use still binds the tenant. If you will allow child care, use the optional child care clause to set conditions such as registration, a limit on the number of children and liability insurance.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText:
Farm leases have their own rules. If you rent a home that comes with land or water, no West Virginia statute says whether hunting, fishing or trapping rights go to the tenant or stay with you, so the lease decides. Three rules in the wildlife law matter. Hunting, fishing or trapping on fenced, enclosed or posted land of another person needs the permission of the owner, the tenant or the owner's agent, and the hunter should carry it in writing; doing it without permission is a misdemeanor, and the hunter is liable for damage such as harm to animals or fences.

The owner, a lessee or another person entitled to possession may post unenclosed land against hunting, trapping and fishing. And a bona fide resident tenant, meaning one who lives permanently on the land, may hunt, trap and fish on that land in season without a license, unless the land is a wildlife refuge or preserve. Because your tenant can lawfully give strangers permission to hunt on the land, add a lease term if you want to control it; the library's optional hunting and fishing consent clause does this.

title: Plain Language: No Waiver Statement or Readability Test
bodyText: West Virginia's plain-language law applies to residential leases: a written agreement for renting space to live in must use clear, everyday words, readable type and ink that contrasts with the paper, and sections organized and captioned so they are easy to understand (see the plain language row). It is simpler than the plain-language laws of some states. It sets no readability score or test, it does not require the lease to include a statement listing the rights the tenant gives up or what the tenant could lose by not meeting the lease's obligations, there is no process for having a lease approved in advance by the Attorney General, and there is no exclusion for leases above a dollar amount. Words that a state or federal law requires or permits may be used. A lease that falls short is not void, but if the tenant asks for a conforming lease and you refuse, the tenant can sue to have it rewritten, and the tenant cannot waive that right. You may add a plain summary of the main obligations if you wish; keep it accurate and consistent with the lease.

title: Recycling and Trash at Rentals
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to provide recycling at a rental or to tell tenants where and how to recycle. Recycling is run by local government. Every city of 10,000 or more people must have a curbside program, with an ordinance requiring each person and business in the city to separate at least three kinds of recyclable materials, and the city itself must tell everyone occupying homes and other premises in the city how the program works.
