A county may also adopt a program requiring everyone who subscribes to a trash collection service to separate recyclables. Those local rules bind you and your tenants directly, so check the city or county program and, if you arrange trash service, tell tenants how it works and put any rules in the lease. Separately, every person occupying a residence must either subscribe to and pay for a solid waste collection service or be able to prove proper disposal at least once every 30 days, and failing to can bring a civil penalty and a misdemeanor charge; the lease should say whether you or the tenant arranges and pays for trash service. In a building with more than one dwelling unit, you must provide and maintain appropriate conveniences for removing garbage, rubbish and other waste.

title: No State Tenant Rights Guide to Hand Over
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to give a tenant a state-published guide to tenant rights and responsibilities, before the lease is signed or at renewal, or to have the tenant sign an acknowledgment that they received one. No state agency is directed to publish such a guide for private rentals. This matches the rule that you need not give a tenant a state summary of tenant rights or a copy of the landlord-tenant statutes (see the tenant rights statement row). The one written notice of tenant rights the law does require in a rental setting is narrow: if a building is converted to a condominium or other common interest community, the declarant or dealer must give each residential tenant a notice of the conversion that sets out the tenants' rights, at least 120 days before the tenants must leave. If you choose to give tenants a summary of the lease or of the law, make sure it is accurate and does not contradict the lease.

title: No Occupancy Notice or First-Page Rule for House Leases
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires a lease of a single-family home, or any residential lease, to carry a notice about who is presumed to have a lawful right to occupy, to be notarized or signed by a licensed property manager, or to put any disclosure on the first page or in larger type than the rest of the lease. What West Virginia does have is the Stop Squatters Act: a squatter is someone occupying a dwelling who is not entitled to under a rental or lease agreement and is not authorized by the tenant or owner, and the quick police removal it allows is not available against a current or former lawful tenant. When an owner asks for removal, the officer may look at any lease the occupant claims to have. So sign a written lease with every tenant, keep a copy, and name every adult who may live there; it is the simplest proof of who is a tenant and who is not. For type size, the plain-language rule applies: the lease must use readable type (see the type-size row).

title: No Shoreline or Water-Access Disclosure
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule requires you to tell a tenant about public access to a shoreline, beach, river or lake next to a rental, about riparian (waterfront) rights that go with the property, or about limits on the tenant's own access to the water. West Virginia's rules about shores and waterways deal with matters such as boating speeds near a shoreline, public fishing and boating access sites, state park beaches, and the taking of land or water rights for public projects; they bind whoever uses the water or the agency involved, not landlords as such. If your rental is on a lake or river and the tenant may use a dock, beach or the water, the lease can say what the tenant may use and on what rules, as an ordinary term you choose to include. For flood risk, see the flood row.

title: Renting a House in a Single-Family Zone
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or rule limits renting out a house in a single-family zone to owners who live on the lot, and the state has no lot-split or two-unit program that makes an owner live in one unit or limits how the units are rented. State law leans the other way. A statute in the Municipal Home Rule Program section says municipalities may not prohibit or effectively limit the rental of a property, or regulate the duration, frequency or location of rentals, though they may regulate activities that arise from rental use if the rule applies the same way to every property, rented or not; whether that reaches every city, and how far it goes, is unsettled. Since June 4, 2026, a city or town must also allow at least one accessory dwelling unit by right on a lot with a single-family house and may not require a family, marital or employment relationship between the people living in the house and in the accessory unit, though it may still regulate short-term rentals (see the accessory dwelling unit row). Check county and city zoning ordinances, and any deed restrictions or association rules on your lot, before you rent.

title: Renting to Students
bodyText: West Virginia has no special rules for renting to students: no student-housing license or certification, and no separate landlord-tenant regime. A house or apartment you rent to students is an ordinary tenancy under the general landlord-tenant, security deposit and eviction laws, none of which exempts student housing, and because West Virginia has no rent-cap or just-cause eviction law, there is no dormitory exemption to sort out. College residence halls are run by the colleges themselves, with rooms and fees set by their governing boards, and the special trespass rule for residence halls covers only housing a college owns, operates or controls. Being a student is not one of the traits West Virginia's fair housing law protects, but a students-only policy can shut out families with children, whom the law does protect, so apply your screening rules to every applicant. A person 18 or older can sign a lease like any adult; whether a lease signed by a younger student binds them is a question for case law, so have a parent or guardian sign as a tenant or as a written guarantor. For roommates, a joint-and-several liability term makes each signer answerable for the whole rent.

title: Housing Your Own Employee
bodyText: West Virginia has no special rules for housing your own employee or caretaker: no required disclosure of when the employee must leave, no duty to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, and no filing for housing a sponsored or guest worker. The landlord-tenant, security deposit and eviction laws have no exclusion for housing an employer provides, so treat an employee who lives in your property as a tenant and put the arrangement in a written lease (see the scope row). Whether an occupancy tied only to the job is a tenancy at all is a question for case law. The eviction statutes do not name caretakers or employees: summary eviction is for removing a tenant, and unlawful detainer reaches a tenant who stays after the right to possession has ended. If an employee or former employee will not leave, use the court process; the police-removal procedure of the Stop Squatters Act is not for a person you authorized to live there or for a current or former lawful tenant. A lease term that ends the tenancy when the job ends is not offered by this library, because whether it works depends on how courts read the notice rules and the job-tied occupancy question; you may add your own term with a lawyer's advice. Separately, the minimum wage law allows an employer a reasonable credit for lodging furnished to an employee under the Labor Commissioner's rules. Farm worker housing is outside this library.

title: Animals Left in a Rental
bodyText:
West Virginia gives you no special right to enter a rental to feed, check on or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. No statute treats a person who feeds or shelters an animal for a set number of days as its owner. The dog and rabies laws do place duties on anyone who owns, keeps or harbors a dog or cat, such as rabies vaccination and ten days' confinement after a bite, without defining those words or setting a time, so if you take an animal in, you may have those duties while you have it.

No statute sets when you may enter a rental at all, so your entry rights come from the lease (see "Landlord Entry"). It is a crime for any person intentionally, knowingly or recklessly to abandon an animal or to withhold food, water, shelter or necessary medical treatment from it. The county humane officer (a deputy sheriff, or the dog warden, designated for the job) must take possession of an animal known or believed to be abandoned or neglected, and anyone may report such an animal to a humane officer without civil or criminal liability for the report.

If you find an animal left without care, try the tenant and any caretaker the tenant named, then call the humane officer or the police rather than keeping, rehoming or disposing of the animal yourself. The steps for belongings left by a tenant who abandons while owing rent, and for belongings left after an eviction order, speak of personal property; West Virginia law calls a dog personal property, but those steps say nothing about feeding and sheltering a living animal during the notice period, so do not treat an animal like furniture.

The optional animal-care clause ("Animal Care in Tenant's Absence" clause) has the tenant list every animal and name a caretaker you may let in if the tenant is hospitalized, detained or otherwise away; it ends at the tenant's death, after which you deal with the heirs or personal representative. Counties may adopt their own ordinances on the custody and care of abandoned or neglected animals; check yours.

title: Housing People Displaced by a Disaster
bodyText: West Virginia has no law letting a tenant take in people displaced by a flood, fire or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy terms, none limiting such stays, and none saying when a displaced person staying in a hotel, a short-term rental or a tenant's home becomes a tenant. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms apply (see "Guests' Rights" and the guest clauses tagged for West Virginia), and fair housing law still bars occupancy rules that discriminate because of familial status, disability or another protected class. During a state of emergency or state of preparedness proclaimed by the Governor or the Legislature, the Governor may control the movement of people and the occupancy of premises in the affected area, order evacuations and provide for the care of evacuees, and make provision for temporary emergency housing; follow any executive order that reaches your property. In the declared area, rent for month-to-month housing may not rise more than 10 percent above what you charged on the 10th day before the declaration, apart from a narrow cost exception (see "Rent Limits During a Declared Emergency"); the cautious course is to treat a new charge for extra occupants of a month-to-month unit as part of that price. If a tenant asks to house displaced family or friends, give a written consent naming the people, the number allowed and an end date, and keep a copy. A person the tenant authorized, or a member of the tenant's immediate family, cannot be removed by the police under the Stop Squatters Act, so a guest who stays past the end date is handled under the lease and, if needed, an eviction case against the tenant. Hotels, motels and other short-stay lodging are outside this library.

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations
bodyText: West Virginia has not moved or renumbered its protective-order laws since it recodified its domestic relations chapter in 2001. Domestic violence protective orders still issue under chapter 48, article 27 of the Code, and personal safety orders, for people the domestic violence article does not cover, under chapter 53, article 8. A 2026 law on military interpersonal violence amended some of these sections, and the current definitions include a military protective order issued by a commanding officer, but the articles kept their numbers. What did move was fair housing: in 2024 the West Virginia Fair Housing Act moved from chapter 5, article 11A to chapter 16B, article 18, and the Human Rights Act from chapter 5, article 11 to chapter 16B, article 17, and the old articles now print as repealed (see "West Virginia Fair Housing Act"). The West Virginia rows in this library cite the current numbering. For you as a landlord, the substance is what matters: a domestic violence protective order may give the petitioner possession of the home the parties shared and order the respondent to stay away from it, but it cannot affect title to real property, and protection orders from other states, territories and tribes are enforced in West Virginia (see "Domestic Violence and the Tenancy" and "Lock Changes and Protective Orders"). If a form, policy or guide you use cites the fair housing law in chapter 5, or predates the 2001 recodification, update it.

title: Screening Your Staff
bodyText: West Virginia does not require you, at any size of property, to run background checks on maintenance workers, leasing agents, property managers or contractors who have keys to or enter tenants' units, and no state statute generally forbids or limits asking a job applicant about criminal history for this kind of work. A few rules reach every employer. You may not require or ask an employee or job applicant, directly or indirectly, to take a lie detector or similar test; the exceptions (jobs with direct access to controlled substances, law enforcement and the state's military forces) do not cover property staff, and a violation is a misdemeanor and lets the person sue for three times the damages plus attorney fees and costs. A person whose conviction a court has expunged does not have to disclose it on a job application. If you employ 12 or more people in West Virginia for 20 or more weeks in the year, the Human Rights Act bars discrimination in hiring and bars application forms that ask about race, religion, color, national origin, ancestry, sex or age, so apply any screening evenly. If you turn down an applicant or take other adverse action based on a report from a screening company, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's adverse-action notice applies to employment decisions as well as rentals (see "Federal Notice When a Screening Report Leads to a Denial"); before you get a screening report on a job applicant or employee, the Act requires you to give them a clear written notice, in a document containing only that notice, that a report may be obtained, and to get their written permission; before you act against them because of the report, give them a copy of it and the federal summary of their rights. Screening anyone you give keys or codes is still sound practice, alongside key control (see the library's key-control row); whether an owner can be liable for harm a staff member causes is a question for case law.

title: Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Terms
bodyText: West Virginia has no rule requiring the same rent or the same terms for a month-to-month (or other periodic) tenancy and a fixed-term lease, and no cap on how much the rent you offer for the two may differ. You may price and write them differently, as long as the difference is not based on race, familial status, disability or another class protected by fair housing law. Several rules do turn on the type of tenancy. To end a periodic tenancy, either side gives written notice of at least one full rental period before the end of a period (three months before the end of a year for a year-to-year tenancy), unless the lease fixes another period; a lease ending on a set date needs no notice under state law, though on a property covered by the federal CARES Act federal law bars requiring the tenant to vacate until 30 days after a notice to vacate, so give at least 30 days' written notice (see "Notice to End a Tenancy" and "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties"). During a declared state of emergency or preparedness, the 10 percent price cap reaches rental housing leased month-to-month, not fixed-term leases (see "Rent Limits During a Declared Emergency"). After a trustee's sale under a deed of trust, the buyer may end a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy on 30 days' written notice, while a tenant with an unexpired written lease that is unrecorded or was recorded after the deed of trust gets 90 days' written notice or written notice at least 30 days before the lease ends, whichever is shorter (see "Tenants After a Trustee's Sale"). Local hotel occupancy tax does not reach sleeping accommodations rented month-to-month or for 30 days or longer from the start (see "Taxes on Rent"). The security deposit, late-fee and repair rules apply to every residential tenancy alike.

title: Parking Rules and Towing From Your Lot
bodyText:
West Virginia has no statute on how you deliver or label parking or towing rules, whether you may change them during the lease, what vehicle information you may ask a tenant for, or whether a parking permit must run with the lease, and none requires the lease to say whether parking is included or what it costs. No statute gives a resident a waiting period or posted notice before a tow for expired registration or inspection, and none requires towing signs at a private residential lot. Two state rules govern removing a vehicle.

A driver may not stop, park or leave a vehicle on private property without the express or implied permission of the owner, tenant or lessee; the owner, tenant or lessee may move the vehicle or have it moved without paying for the move and is not liable for damage done in moving it unless negligent, the vehicle's owner owes the removal costs, and whoever removes the vehicle must notify the State Police and, inside a city or town, the municipal police.

A tow done without the vehicle owner's consent may be performed only by a wrecker company authorized by the Public Service Commission, which may charge only its approved rates and must mail an itemized invoice to the vehicle's registered owner within 15 days of the tow (30 days for a vehicle registered in another state). A tenant's car parked where the lease allows is parked with permission, so put your parking rules in the lease or a signed addendum and say where tenants and guests may park; the optional clause "Vehicles Parked Without Permission" does this and adds written notice before a tenant's own car is towed.

A parking charge the lease sets is rent in this library (see topic `unbundled-parking`), so don't add or raise one during a fixed term unless the lease allows it (see "Raising Rent During a Lease Term"), and change parking rules in a periodic tenancy with the notice described in "Changing Terms of a Periodic Tenancy". A parking rule should not bar a lawfully possessed firearm kept out of view and locked in a vehicle (see "Firearms"). Abandoned vehicles are covered in "Towing and Abandoned Vehicles".

Counties and cities may regulate parking and towing locally; check yours.

title: Acts Tenants Must Not Commit
bodyText:
West Virginia has no statute listing the acts a residential tenant must not commit, and no crime aimed at tenants as such, so your lease supplies those rules; the library's Prohibited Acts by Tenant clause covers damaging the property, disturbing others and unreasonably refusing entry. Several laws back the lease up. You may file for summary eviction when the tenant has breached a lease covenant, or has deliberately or negligently damaged the property or knowingly permitted another person to do so. A tenant who commits waste on the property while in possession, without your special permission, is liable for the damage.

General criminal laws reach tenants as they reach anyone: unlawfully destroying, injuring or defacing another person's property is a misdemeanor, and doing it willfully and intentionally with a loss of $2,500 or more is a felony; a squatter who damages the property commits criminal mischief; and if you run a lodging or boarding house, obtaining lodging with intent to defraud you, or absconding without paying, is a misdemeanor. Disabling fire warning systems and smoke detector duties are covered in "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors" and under topic `alarm-tampering-fee`, and the tenant's other statutory duties in "Tenant Duties Set by Statute".

title: When Unlawful Use Voids the Lease
bodyText: One West Virginia statute voids a lease because of how the property is used. Every lease or other agreement, written or oral, to let, sublet or rent a house, building or other structure that is used for prostitution, lewdness or assignation is void from the date any party to the agreement is convicted under the prostitution statute. A conviction is needed, of the tenant or of anyone else who is a party to the lease, and it is the statute, not your lease, that ends it. Letting a place when you know or have good reason to know the tenant means to use it for prostitution is itself a crime, and anyone who maintains such a place, including its owner or lessee, can be sued to abate it as a nuisance; the court can close the place for a year, and an owner who shows good faith and no knowledge of the use can get it released by posting bond. No other West Virginia statute voids a lease, or returns possession to you, because the tenant uses the property for another unlawful purpose such as drug dealing or gambling. For those uses rely on the lease: the residential-use covenant tagged for West Virginia and the optional criminal-activity clause make illegal use a breach of a lease covenant, which is a ground for summary eviction. Real property used to commit or help commit a drug felony can be forfeited to the state, but not to the extent of the interest of an owner who shows the use happened without the owner's knowledge or consent, so act promptly when you learn of drug activity. A court may also order the owner or lessee of premises used by an organized criminal enterprise to remove or evict the people using it. Even when a conviction voids the lease, remove an occupant who stays through the courts, not by changing the locks (see "Lockouts and Utility Shutoffs").

title: Smoke Drifting Between Units
bodyText:
West Virginia has no statute or state rule on tobacco smoke drifting between units, no statewide indoor smoking ban that reaches apartment common areas, no required smoking-policy disclosure, and no rule on a lease term in which a tenant accepts drifting smoke or gives up claims about it. The one general statewide workplace smoking law makes it a misdemeanor to smoke in a factory, mercantile establishment, mill or workshop that posts a no-smoking notice at its main entrances; it does not reach apartment hallways where your staff work. Smoking at your building is therefore governed by your lease.

The library's Smoking Policy clause bans smoking, including marijuana and vaping, everywhere on the property, and a building-wide ban is the surest way to prevent drift (see "Smoking, Vaping and Medical Cannabis"). If you allow smoking in some units or areas, the optional clause "Smoke From Other Units or Areas" tells the tenant before signing that smoke may drift from them. The library does not offer a clause in which the tenant waives claims over drifting smoke: no West Virginia statute permits such a waiver, the state Constitution guarantees every person a remedy for an injury, and how courts treat liability waivers in leases is case law (see "Liability Waivers"); if you want one, have a lawyer draft it.

If your staff smoke, remember that an employer may not refuse to hire or penalize an employee solely for using tobacco off the employer's premises during nonworking hours. Local board of health rules and ordinances may restrict smoking in common areas; check yours.

title: Tenant Insurance and Fire Claims
bodyText: No West Virginia statute says whether you may require a tenant to file a claim on the tenant's renter's insurance, or may file a claim against the tenant's policy yourself. None bars you or your insurer from suing a tenant over an accidental fire, and none addresses a lease term in which you and the tenant waive claims against each other for losses insurance covers (a mutual waiver or waiver of subrogation). Three statutes set the frame. A tenant's promise to leave the premises in good repair does not make the tenant rebuild, or pay for, buildings destroyed by fire or otherwise without the tenant's fault or negligence, unless other words in the lease show that the parties meant it to. When buildings are destroyed without the tenant's fault or negligence, the tenant gets a reasonable rent reduction unless the lease provides otherwise, and may leave if you do not rebuild within a reasonable time (see "Fire or Casualty Damage" clause). And your repair duties for residential property stay with you, so do not make a repair you owe depend on the tenant's insurance claim (see "Landlord's Repair Duties"). Whether a tenant who carelessly causes a fire is liable to you, or to your insurer after it pays you, is a question for case law. The library's damage clause charges the tenant only for damage caused by the tenant, a family member or a guest through a deliberate or negligent act or a lack of reasonable care (see "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause), and its insurance clause requires renter's insurance without a landlord-not-liable sentence (see "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause). The library does not offer a mutual waiver of insured losses, because for the tenant it releases claims against you, release terms are kept out of this library's West Virginia clauses, and their enforceability is case law (see "Liability Waivers"); if you want one, have your insurer and a lawyer review it.

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText:
West Virginia has no statute on tenant portals, the websites or apps you may use for applications, rent, repair requests and documents. No statute bars requiring rent to be paid electronically, so the lease's payment terms govern (see "How Rent May Be Paid"). Signatures and documents are different. The electronic transactions act applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, judged from the context and the parties' conduct, and a party who agreed may refuse to conduct later transactions electronically; that right cannot be waived. So a lease can record the tenant's agreement to sign and receive documents through your portal, but it cannot stop the tenant from switching to paper for future transactions.

Federal law likewise does not require anyone to agree to use electronic records. Where a law requires information to be given to the tenant in writing, a portal document counts only if the tenant can print or store it, and if the law requires a particular method, such as mail or posting, you must still use that method; consumer-consent steps may also apply to information a law requires you to give in writing.

Notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of the tenant's primary residence are outside the act's electronic-records rules (its article 1), so give those on paper by the method the law or the lease sets (see "Electronic Leases and Records" and "Delivering Notices"). The cautious course on fees: do not charge a fee for using a portal you require; if a card or other payment option in the portal carries a fee, keep a no-fee way to pay. The optional clause "Online Tenant Portal" sets up portal use on these terms.

title: Tenant Records and Data
bodyText: West Virginia sets only a few record duties for a residential landlord. You must keep an itemized record, for each tenant, of every deduction you make from a security deposit because the tenant did not comply with the lease, for one year after the tenancy ends, and within 72 hours of a written request, during normal business hours, either let the tenant (or the tenant's authorized agent or attorney) inspect it or, at your option, give them a copy (see "Holding a Deposit and Keeping Records"). If a tenant claims the state's senior homestead tax relief as a renter, you must sign, on request, a statement of the gross rent the tenant paid for the year; willfully refusing or giving a false statement is a misdemeanor (see "Rent Statement for Senior Tax Relief"). No statute requires you to keep a rent ledger, to give a tenant a ledger or payment history on request, or to give rent receipts (see "No Rent Receipt Requirement"), so keep one anyway: a clear ledger is your best evidence in an eviction case. If you keep applicants' or tenants' names together with Social Security numbers, driver's license or state ID numbers, or financial account or card numbers in unencrypted, unredacted computer files, the breach-notice law reaches you as an individual or entity that owns or licenses that data (see "Tenant Information and Data Breaches"). West Virginia has no statute requiring a landlord to adopt a written information-security program or to destroy applicant or tenant records in a particular way; the State's safeguarding rule covers insurance licensees, not landlords. Federal rules also require anyone who keeps tenant screening reports or information from them for business to dispose of them with reasonable measures, such as shredding paper and erasing electronic files so they cannot be read or rebuilt. The cautious course is to collect only what you need, keep paper files locked and electronic files encrypted, and shred or securely delete screening reports and copies of identification when you no longer need them.

title: Binding Arbitration in a Lease
bodyText:
West Virginia's Revised Uniform Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable, except on grounds that would let any contract be revoked. The Act has no exception for leases, consumer contracts or injury claims. Some of the Act's protections can't be given up before a dispute arises, including each party's right to be represented by a lawyer licensed in West Virginia. A court that orders arbitration must pause any related court case.

The library offers an optional arbitration clause for money disputes. It keeps eviction cases, and any rent or damages claimed with them, in court, so the 5-to-10-judicial-day eviction hearing isn't delayed. It also keeps security deposit claims, injury claims, emergency relief and agency complaints out of arbitration, and it lets the tenant reject the clause within 30 days of signing. The clause takes effect only if both parties initial it. West Virginia has no court called a small claims court. Its magistrate courts hear civil claims up to $20,000 and all wrongful-occupation cases, so whether the clause's small-claims carve-out reaches a magistrate-court money claim is unsettled. The cautious course is to join any rent or damages claim to the eviction case in magistrate court, which the clause keeps in court; a money claim brought on its own, such as rent owed after the tenant has moved out, may have to be arbitrated if the tenant asks. Whether West Virginia's courts would enforce an arbitration clause in a residential lease is a question of case law, which wasn't checked here. A landlord who wants different terms can add their own clause with legal advice.

title: No EV Charger Move-Out Rule
bodyText: No West Virginia statute says what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends. If you approve a charger, the lease's alterations terms govern: an approved alteration stays with the property unless you require its removal. Put removal, restoration and who owns the equipment in writing when you give consent.

title: No EV Charger Rules for Rentals
bodyText: No West Virginia statute or agency rule sets requirements for an electric vehicle charger at a rental property. That covers registration or accuracy rules for chargers, a tax on charging sold to tenants, and EV-ready parking. The State Building Code adopts the 2018 International Building Code and International Residential Code by reference; check with your local code official before new construction. Whether billing tenants for the electricity a charger uses is a resale of electricity depends on Commission decisions (see "Reselling Electricity or Gas to Tenants"). The Commission's rules bar a utility from furnishing electricity to a customer for resale unless the customer is itself in the business of distributing electricity as a public utility. The cautious course is to put the charger on a utility meter in the tenant's own name or include charging in the rent, and not to bill tenants by the amount of electricity used without the Commission's or a lawyer's confirmation.

title: No Shared-Area EV Charging Rule
bodyText: No West Virginia statute gives a tenant a right to install or use an electric vehicle charger in a shared parking area or garage, or sets rules for one you provide. A charger in a common area is your decision under the lease's alterations and common-area terms.

title: No Political Sign or Canvassing Rule
bodyText: No West Virginia statute gives a tenant a right to put up political or campaign signs despite the lease, or gives candidates or canvassers a right to enter a rental building or complex. Your lease's sign and common-area rules govern. Apply them the same way to everyone (see the row on flags, signs and other displays).

title: No Religious Display Right
bodyText: No West Virginia statute gives a tenant a right to display a religious or cultural item, such as a symbol on the door frame, despite a lease restriction. The lease's display terms govern. But you may not set or enforce display rules differently because of a tenant's religion or national origin: the fair housing law bars different terms or conditions on those grounds.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: West Virginia follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (W. Va. Code § 46-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (W. Va. Code § 46-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was sent to a lock box for payments of undisputed claims. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: West Virginia's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (W. Va. Code ch. 37 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how West Virginia's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
